stories.body:
Search and rescue efforts under way after quake strikes region’s north, officials say, while at least seven aftershocks recorded

A magnitude-7 earthquake has hit China’s Tibet region, killing at least 16 people, injuring 54 and collapsing hundreds of homes in the northern regional city of Nagqu, official media said.

Search and rescue efforts continued after the collapse of at least 339 homes and 20 livestock sheds, the Nagqu media office said, citing city government officials.

More than 1,600 people from the local county were deployed for rescue efforts. Supplies including 1,000 prefabricated housing units and about 3,000 tents and folding beds as well as torches and winter clothing arrived in the region.

The US Geological Survey said the quake occurred at 10.33pm local time on Thursday, with its epicentre 191km (119 miles) east-northeast of Nagqu, in a sparsely populated, high-altitude area of northern Tibet . It put the earthquake’s depth at 18km.

The US agency recorded at least seven aftershocks with magnitude between 4.3 and 5.2, all of them with a depth of 10km, according to its website.

Videos posted by China’s national broadcaster CCTV said showed workers running out of restaurants and objects falling off shelves at supermarkets when the quake struck.

China’s official Xinhua news agency said on Friday that communication in some areas hit by the quake was down. Local railway authorities had taken emergency actions to halt trains passing through the region.

More than 300 police officers had been dispatched for relief work while the regional fire and rescue corps has mobilised almost 350 personnel to the affected areas, Xinhua reported.

Rescue workers clambered through damaged buildings, some with collapsed roofs, footage on CCTV showed.

The earthquake also caused rockfalls that had forced local authorities to close a section of national highway 317, allowing only emergency, rescue and official support vehicles through as crews worked to clear debris, according to Xinhua.

Intermittent snows were expected in the quake region over the next three days, Xinhua said. It was the biggest quake in the region in the past five years, CCTV said.

China’s leader, Xi Jinping, called for all-out efforts in rescue operations and medical relief work.

Nagqu is more than 300km north of Tibet’s capital, Lhasa.

Earthquakes are relatively common in China. In January 2025, at least 126 people were killed in one in Tibet’s rural Tingri county.

In December 2023, a quake in remote Gansu province in north-west China killed at least 134 people, state media said. That quake was China’s deadliest since 2014, when more than 600 people died in the south-western province of Yunnan.

A huge tremor in Sichuan province in 2008 left approximately 90,000 people dead or missing, including about 5,000 schoolchildren.

stories.title: "Disillusioned" MAHA leader quits as Trump admin's food agenda spoils: Report
stories.summary: The departure comes amid turmoil in Kennedy's Make America Healthy Again movement.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The departure comes amid turmoil in Kennedy’s Make America Healthy Again movement.

Calley Means—a top ally to anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and a co-author of the so-called “MAHA bible”—resigned from his role in the Trump administration Thursday, reportedly in frustration over delays to food policy changes sought by the Make America Healthy Again movement.

“I am resigning from the White House with tremendous respect for President Trump and Bobby Kennedy,” Means wrote in a social media post this afternoon . “It was an honor to advocate for MAHA moms in the administration and steer policies like Dietary Guidelines reform, psychedelic reform, removing soda from SNAP, removing food dyes, GRAS reform, and overhauling government food procurement.”

His post did not provide a reason for his departure. Means served as a senior advisor to Kennedy.

Sources close to Means told The Wall Street Journal that he had grown frustrated in the position. Means reportedly blamed other members of the administration for allowing the food industry and special interests to have too much sway in policy decisions. One source described Means as “disillusioned.”

The Journal recently reported that the White House had punted on two of Kennedy’s food priorities: defining and regulating ultraprocessed foods, and regulations that would require school meals to have more protein and less sugar. In recent meetings, Means reportedly raised his voice and grew visibly frustrated over the lack of progress on such issues. Others in the administration complained he was unwilling to make political concessions.

Means’ resignation comes as members of the MAHA movement have grown increasingly critical of Kennedy’s inability to follow through with key policy priorities. There is also growing backlash to Kennedy’s seeming embrace of corporate interests. A MAHA summit last month drew scorn for having numerous corporate sponsors, including Walmart, UnitedHealth, Anthropic, OpenAI, and Grail. Sponsorship packages were reportedly sold for up to $300,000. At the summit, Kennedy sat down for a “fireside chat” with Vice President JD Vance and extolled the potential of artificial intelligence. Many MAHA members and leaders felt betrayed by the corporate involvement, saying it was antithetical to the grassroots nature of the MAHA movement.

Means is among the early leaders of the grassroots effort. Along with his sister, Casey Means , he co-authored a book considered the “MAHA bible,” titled Good Energy: The Surprising Connection Between Metabolism and Limitless Health . The book provides a potpourri of dietary and lifestyle advice, including recommendations to avoid processed foods, seed oils, fragrances, various home care products, fluoride, unfiltered water, bananas (when eaten alone), receipt paper, and birth control pills. One of its chapters is titled “Trust Yourself, Not Your Doctor.”

Trump nominated Casey Means to be surgeon general, but her nomination was abandoned amid misgivings over her medical qualifications, positions on vaccines, and promotion of unproven wellness claims.

stories.title: No order, no seat: Starbucks China rolls out new store policy
stories.summary: Starbucks says it is improving customers' in-store experience as it competes with homegrown rivals.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
"Purchase to sit" signs are popping up in Starbucks stores around China

Published 22 October 2026

Taking a seat at a Starbucks in China? Just make sure you're also ordering something there.

A new policy by Starbucks China takes effect across all its 8,000 stores on Thursday, making it mandatory for people to purchase items if they want to sit in its cafes.

Starbucks China said the move was part of efforts to improve the "in-store experience" for customers. The company is facing stiff competition from homegrown brands such as Luckin Coffee.

Starbucks stores around the world have also been wrestling with non-paying seat-hoggers and other undesirable behaviour from customers.

In South Korea, Starbucks has told customers to stop bringing "bulky items" into their stores , after some patrons reportedly hogged seats with printers and desktop computers in tow.

In North America, Starbucks reversed its open-door policy which for years allowed people to use their seats and toilets without buying anything, saying that it wanted to "prioritise" paying customers.

Starbucks China is now following suit.

Ahead of the official announcement on Wednesday, reports of the new seating policy at China's Starbucks stores had been circulating this week - along with social media videos of what appear to be "purchase to sit" signs in Starbucks stores.

Many on Chinese social media welcomed the new policy.

"Finally, there won't be peak periods where people are just sitting there not ordering anything, drinking Luckin coffee, playing games and yelling on the phone," reads one of the top-liked comment on Weibo. "Every time I walk around, there's nowhere to sit,"

"There's nothing wrong with it. I'd feel awkward sitting there if I didn't make a purchase. I'd rather leave the seats for those who made purchases and need the seats," another Weibo user commented.

Last month, a Starbucks store in Sichuan province sparked debate after video of its chained-up outdoor seats and tables were circulated on social media. It appeared to be an attempt to block people from sitting there without paying.

Since opening its first store there in 1999, China has become Starbucks' second-largest market. But it has faced stiff competition in recent years from Luckin and other local brands that offer cheaper products.

Luckin also offers a robust app-based ordering system that prioritises grab-and-go transactions, challenging Starbucks' model of a full cafe experience where people can sit down and enjoy their food and drinks.

In 2023, Luckin overtook Starbucks as China's largest coffee chain.

Starbucks said last year it would sell 60% stake of its business in China as part of a $4bn (£3.04bn) deal with investment firm Boyu Capital.

In another statement on Wednesday, Starbucks China said it was planning to increase staffing and improve digital systems at its stores, among other investments to "ensure customers receive timely and warm service even during peak hours".

stories.body:
Economic fallout from war in Middle East adds to pressures on consumers and on chancellor before budget

Consumer confidence in the UK has fallen at the fastest rate outside the Covid pandemic since the 2016 Brexit vote as the escalating economic damage from the war in the Middle East hits Britain.

With less than a week before John Healey’s first budget, the latest barometer from the data company GfK indicated confidence plunged by 11 percentage points in October to -24 amid pressure on consumers from the rising cost of living.

Highlighting the challenge for Andy Burnham and his chancellor before the statement on Wednesday, GfK said its consumer confidence index last fell by this much in a single month in July 2016, following the shock leave result in the EU referendum.

The index – which has been closely tracked by the government and the Bank of England for early warning signs from the economy since the early 1970s – recorded its largest ever fall, of 25 points, in March 2020 just after the start of the first UK lockdown.

The latest snapshot represents a marked change from the summer, when GfK said a “ Burnham bounce ”, along with a strong World Cup run by the men’s England football team and sunny weather, lifted the mood of consumers in its long-running monthly survey.

Neil Bellamy, consumer insights director at GfK, said: “Relentless cost-of-living pressures, against an international backdrop of unresolved regional conflicts that are themselves contributing to domestic inflation now at 3.5%, appear to have swept aside the nascent optimism we saw following the appointment of a new UK prime minister this summer.”

It comes as consumers face a fresh squeeze on living standards triggered by the unfolding war in the Middle East. Petrol and diesel prices have surged close to record highs and energy bills have increased in advance of a difficult winter for households already feeling the pinch from years of price increases.

Over the past five years analysis by the Trades Union Congress shows that UK households have paid almost £14,000 on average in additional costs for mortgages, loans, energy and water bills.

With less than a week before his tax and spending speech to the Commons, the chancellor is under pressure to take action to support households amid warnings that consumer energy bills could reach £2,000 a year from January for the typical household.

Healey has pledged to use his statement to announce “breathing space” measures to ease the pressure. However, he has also warned that the government has limited resources to intervene as the Middle East conflict pushes the UK’s borrowing costs to the highest level in decades.

Official figures released on Wednesday show headline inflation rose by more than expected to 3.5% last month , while the government deficit was a worse-than-forecast £24.5bn.

In a double blow for the chancellor, the twin pieces of bad news underscore the fact that consumers are facing a renewed cost of living squeeze, just as Healey is also under increased financial pressure.

According to the latest figures from GfK, consumers became less confident about the strength of their own personal finances, as well as the general outlook for the British economy at large.

The major purchase index fell by 14 points to -22 in October, suggesting that consumers could be bracing to cut back on spending over the winter months to make room in their finances for higher energy bills.

Separate figures from the CBI show investment intentions among manufacturing businesses were subdued as cost pressures remained high in the three months to October.

Manufacturing output is expected to stabilise in the next three months, according to the lobby group’s latest Industrial Trends Survey. However, cost pressures for businesses remained elevated.

Cameron Martin, senior economist at the CBI, said: “If the government wants to meaningfully tackle the cost of living, it must give manufacturers the breathing space to invest and drive the productivity growth needed to sustain rising real wages.

“Next week’s budget must deliver this by cutting business electricity costs, reducing labour costs and reforming business rates to support rather than hinder investment and growth.”

The Treasury has been approached for comment.

stories.title: UK to draft in military aircraft to fight wildfires, Burnham says
stories.summary: The prime minister is hosting the UK's first wildfire summit to prepare for future blazes after a record summer 2026.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
RAF A400M planes will be able to fight wildfires if fire crews request them

Published 7 hours ago

Military planes and helicopters will be drafted in to tackle wildfires, Prime Minister Andy Burnham is to tell the UK's first summit on the issue.

Civilian fire services in all four nations will be able to request the support of the Royal Air Force's Chinook helicopters and A400M planes to fight wildfires on tough terrain such as remote moorland and steep hillsides.

Burnham said the measures were needed because "we cannot put people through another summer like this one".

The government will host its first "wildfire resilience summit" on Friday to discuss how to prevent, respond to and recover from such blazes after a record-breaking summer 2026.

There have been 1,350 wildfires in England and Wales this year, an all-time high and up by more than 300 on last year and more than 1,000 on 2024, according to figures from the National Fire Chiefs Council .

Records for the number of reported wildfires were also broken in 2022 and 2025 - but the UK's Climate Change Committee has warned the risk will rise in the coming decades.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said this was the first time the RAF's Chinooks and the four-engine A400Ms were being equipped to tackle wildfires. Some areas struggled with no air assistance in the summer.

Chinooks have practised picking up and dropping water from firefighting buckets in Portland harbour, UK

RAF Chinook crews have already helped respond , external to wildfires in Cyprus.

In addition to military aircraft, the government said it would also spend £45m on wildfire-specific personal protective equipment for firefighters on the ground.

It is lighter than current firefighting equipment which is designed for fires in buildings and not meant to be worn for a long time, the government added.

Ministers are also pledging a £25m scheme from April 2027 to April 2029 to restore dried-out peatlands in England so they are natural firebreaks, and financial support for farmers to fireproof their land such as by digging ponds.

"The government will also look at tougher local restrictions or product bans to stop people starting fires when the risk is high," a briefing ahead of the summit said, following a temporary ban on disposable BBQs .

Burnham will meet fire chiefs, local leaders and experts from tech companies at the summit.

"I stood in Stourbridge and watched families lose everything," he said on Thursday, recounting the night of a wildfire that destroyed 19 homes in the West Midlands in August.

"I will never forget it. Our firefighters were heroes that day, but heroes shouldn't have to fight with one hand tied behind their backs."

Earlier this month, MPs on the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs Committee said there were weaknesses in the UK's wildfire preparedness , including access to aerial firefighting resources, securing water supplies during major incidents and coordinating resources at a national level.

Firefighters tackled wildfires across the UK over the summer, including here in Ebbw Vale, Wales

MPs said the current system for obtaining aerial firefighting support was "no longer fit for purpose".

At the summit, a "Wildfires AI Unit" will be announced to combine universities, tech firms and officials on the Cobra emergency committee, along with Met Office wildfire forecasts and closer work with devolved governments.

In August, the government convened a Cobra meeting before sending an emergency alert to millions of phones across England and Wales - which sparked a backlash from some .

Summer 2026 was the UK's hottest on record, according to the Met Office. In a study on how this summer was impacted by human-induced climate change, it said the heat experienced was made 130 times more likely .

"The wildfires that tore through our countryside this summer showed the urgent need to adapt to our changing climate," Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle said ahead of the summit.

"Nature is our greatest ally in preventing wildfires starting in the first place," she added.

Major incidents were declared for wildfires this year in areas such as Dunwich Heath and RSPB Minsmere in Suffolk, the Cairngorms , Hampshire and Holme Fen in Cambridgeshire.

stories.title: Canadians Are Running Out Of Time To Oppose The Dangerous C-22 Surveillance Bill
stories.summary: Canada’s Parliament is debating a massive expansion of surveillance powers that will threaten the privacy and security of millions of people. Bill C-22, also called the Lawful Access Act, has already passed the House of Commons, and is now before the Canadian Senate. Canadians still have an opportunity to speak out and stop this dangerous legislation. The Canadian Civil Liberties Association (CCLA) is urging all Canadians to sign its petition opposing the bill. (The petition on CCLA’s website is governed by CCLA’s privacy policy.) Take action Tell the canadian senate to stop C-22 As we wrote earlier this year , Bill C-22 gives the government new powers to force digital services—including telecom companies, messaging apps, and more—to help with government surveillance. Worse, it allows Canada’s Minister of Public Safety to order companies to create a backdoor to their services for law enforcement, as long as it doesn’t lead to a “systemic insecurity.” That’s a clear recipe for weakening the encryption we all rely on. It also requires services to retain metadata for up to a year, which reveals who people communicate with, where they go, and what services they use, even when they are not suspected of any crime. Researchers at CCLA and Citizen Lab published a detailed analysis of C-22 and its serious constitutional and cybersecurity problems. The analysis points out that the bill needs more than cosmetic changes—it calls for entirely withdrawing Part 2 of Bill C-22, the section that establishes the surveillance and data retention regime. Bill C-22 could also expand the sharing of Canadians’ personal data with foreign law enforcement, including the United States. Canada has been negotiating a cross-border data-sharing agreement with the U.S. that would allow American police to get information about Canadian internet users without any Canadian court oversight. Some Canadian senators have already expressed concerns about the bill, and rightly suggested, as CCLA and Citizen Lab have, that it may not be compatible with privacy protections in the Canadian constitution. If you’re in Canada, read and sign CCLA’s petition opposing Bill C-22 today. Don’t let the Senate allow this dangerous expansion of government surveillance to become Canada’s new reality. Take action Canadians: defend your privacy and security

stories.title: FCC chair warns media not to run the "fake polls" Trump keeps complaining about
stories.summary: Ex-FCC chairs say Brendan Carr aims to scare broadcasters into self-censorship.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Ex-FCC chairs say Brendan Carr aims to scare broadcasters into self-censorship.

Federal Communications Commission Chairman Brendan Carr today warned broadcasters about airing “fake polls,” amplifying one of the many complaints that President Trump has regularly made about the news media.

Carr’s post on X said, “Many journalists and broadcasters have been amplifying or airing these Polls without regard to basic journalistic ethics and without informing the public that those Polls lack a scientific, accurate, or even real basis… Broadcasters are advised to avoid engaging in News Distortions or running Broadcast Hoaxes by airing Polls that would violate their regulatory obligations.”

Carr urged broadcasters to “provide their viewers with additional context and information about Polls they have covered.” In fact, one small polling outfit was exposed as a hoax this week, and a similar incident occurred in August. News outlets have reported on these hoaxes, providing the very “context” that Carr said is needed.

Carr’s post did not mention any specific fake polls or any specific broadcasters that aired them. The vagueness of Carr’s post may be useful for his and Trump’s ongoing battle against the news media. In August, Trump demanded that the FCC punish or rebuke an NBC journalist for saying he has “mixed results” in election endorsements and wrote that the FCC must do something about “THE FAKE POLLS USED BY OUR CROOKED MEDIA.”

Ex-FCC chairs: Carr wants “self-censorship”

Carr’s latest warning to broadcasters came as no surprise, given that he has spent much of the past two years threatening broadcast licenses and opening investigations into Trump’s least favorite news companies. Former Republican and Democratic FCC chairs and commissioners recently said Carr is seeking to censor and chill the speech of broadcasters through a proceeding that threatens the licenses of ABC-owned stations .

“FCC Chair Brendan Carr’s threat against broadcasters over their reporting on political polls is yet another truly outrageous attempt to censor and control the information available to Americans as they prepare to vote… Carr is now seizing on reports about fabricated political polling as an excuse to once again try to scare broadcasters into self-censorship,” said a statement today from a group of former FCC chairs and officials.

Today’s statement was attributed to former Chairman Tom Wheeler, a Democrat; former Chairman Mark Fowler, a Republican; and seven former high-ranking FCC officials. “Good-faith reporting on public polls—even ones that turn out to be made up—is not a violation of the FCC’s news distortion or hoax rules. And the FCC has zero authority to dictate editorial decisions,” they said.

Wheeler, Fowler, and others previously signed a letter objecting to the ABC investigation. The letter called it “the latest attack in a sustained campaign by Chairman Carr and the Trump administration of threatening legal sanctions against licensees whose speech President Trump dislikes.”

Anna Gomez, the only Democratic commissioner on the current FCC, wrote today that “Pollsters who intentionally mislead the public should answer for it, but broadcasters who report publicly available polling data should never be punished when a poll is wrong. FCC rules on news distortion or hoaxes do not apply to a station that reports this data in good faith.”

Pollster admits hoax

An entity called Wedgewood Polls said yesterday that it published fabricated polling data “to test whether media outlets, aggregators, and commentators would report on data without verifying the source, methodology, or underlying firm legitimacy.” It claimed to be running an experiment on the modern political polling industry.

“Despite having no history, formal credentials, or real data behind the vast majority of our releases, Wedgewood Polling was added to major polling aggregators, including The New York Times, FiftyPlusOne, and VoteHub, and repeatedly treated as a legitimate news source,” the statement said.

Notably, the three polling aggregators mentioned in the statement are not broadcast stations or news networks whose programming is carried on local broadcast stations. That’s relevant because Carr has repeatedly said he merely uses the FCC’s regulatory authority over broadcasters with licenses to use public spectrum, and not media outlets that do not have FCC licenses. Carr’s post yesterday warned broadcasters to “comply with their public interest obligations” under “the terms of their federal licenses.”

While Wedgewood Polls claimed that its data faced no scrutiny from news organizations, FiftyPlusOne said it was preparing to publish an article exposing the fraud and had sent a request for comment to Wedgewood. “They did not respond to our request, but instead posted a public statement on social media admitting that they had been fabricating data,” FiftyPlusOne wrote .

FiftyPlusOne, The New York Times, and VoteHub all say they did some vetting of Wedgewood before deciding to use its polls. FiftyPlusOne wrote:

Their statement alleges that FiftyPlusOne, The New York Times, and other poll aggregators did not conduct appropriate vetting of their firm prior to aggregating their polls; this is false. We reached out to them to ask who they were and confirm the methodology statement on their website. We were given two names, Jack Sims and Andrew Prater. We were able to independently confirm that Sims had previous experience in the polling industry and reviewed their methodology statement in detail. It is not atypical for a pollster to leave an existing firm, form their own, and self-fund some surveys to build reputation; we had no reason at the time to believe this case was any different. Wedgewood operated as if it were a legitimate polling firm, including collecting money from donors to conduct crowd-funded polls, and sharing raw survey data (which we now have confirmed was fraudulent) with FiftyPlusOne on Oct. 15, 2026.

NYT and VoteHub explain poll inclusion

VoteHub Head of Data Science Zachary Donnini said that after talking to Wedgewood’s “head pollster,” Votehub “assigned them a D grade and included their polling data on our site.” Meanwhile, The New York Times updated its polling page with a statement about Wedgewood.

The New York Times said it sends all new pollsters “a series of questions regarding the identities of the pollsters; the methods they were using to draw their sample, contact respondents and weight their polls; and the source of their funding.” Wedgewood answered the questions, and the NYT used 15 of its polls for state and congressional-district races.

The Wedgewood “polls were never included in the tracker or average of President Trump’s approval rating or of the national polls tracking overall preference for control of Congress,” the NYT said.

In the previous incident this year, a group called Median Strategies admitted it faked poll results as part of a “social experiment.” The NYT said it never included that group’s results in its trackers “because the group did not respond to our questions about its methodology.”

Nate Silver removed Wedgewood from his polling site today. Wedgewood polls tended to be about 1 percentage point more favorable for Democrats than other polls, according to Silver .

stories.title: Prepare for supply chain disruption from cyber or climate emergencies, Streeting warns
stories.summary: The defence secretary says the UK needs to be ready for scenarios including impact to essential supply chains.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 22 October 2026

Members of the public and businesses need to think more about how they would cope with natural disasters, cyber-attacks or state-sponsored terrorism, the defence secretary has said.

Wes Streeting warned people needed to be more aware of emerging risks facing the UK and make plans to deal with them.

He added that the government was launching a "national resilience conversation" to raise awareness, including advice for households like stocking up on food, bottled water and first aid supplies.

Streeting also said that cyber incidents - like the recently discovered critical security flaw in the programming language which powers much of the internet - will happen "more and more".

Streeting told BBC One's Question Time that the UK is facing a greater threat to the country, "than we have certainly for most, if not all, of my lifetime".

Speaking to an audience at the UK Gun Hall Plant in Telford earlier on Thursday, where it was announced production of tank gun barrels would return to the UK, he spoke of "everyday challenges" facing households.

He pointed to wildfires burning this summer and the flooding that is expected this winter.

Streeting said the public need to be prepared for "increasingly sophisticated cyber-attacks" on businesses, or supply chain disruption caused by "hostile state actors or terrorists".

The defence secretary referenced the critical security flaw in the PHP programming language which has left organisations around the world scrambling to update their systems.

In the UK, 32 government services were offline while the potential cyber-security issues were addressed.

"It's not just from foreign states engaged in espionage or sabotage; it's also organised criminals," Streeting told Question Time.

"In this world of AI that we live in... it does also present threats if people are innovating and pushing against conventional [cyber] defences."

The defence secretary on Thursday spoke at the opening of the UK Gun Hall Plant in Telford, Shropshire

The government hopes to improve the UK's preparedness for emergencies, such as those caused by increasingly likely severe weather events and cyber-attacks by hostile states.

Incidents could leave the public without access to everyday services such as mains water, sewage, phones and the internet.

The "Be Ready" campaign encourages households to stock up on supplies to survive for three days, including non-perishable food, bottled water, a torch, sleeping bags, and first aid items.

It also suggests having a FM radio for updates during outages, and writing down the frequencies of any national or local radio stations you use for news.

Asked by a Question Time audience member whether the campaign amounted to scaremongering, Streeting said the government want "people to be alert but not alarmed".

He said that there was not a "specific thing we've got in mind" when putting out the advice.

But, he added that the supplies on the list "might help you through some power cuts, or might also help you through if... your local shop's subject to a cyber-attack and your card isn't working at the till".

Security Minister Dan Jarvis MP said the advice will ensure emergency services can prioritise people who need more support during crises, and hopes it will "improve our resilience as a nation".

It follows on from similar campaigns by European countries, like France, Ireland and the Netherlands, where the advice is a "normal part of everyday life", he added.

Last month Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle said people should prepare for extreme weather as the strongest El Niño event in a generation develops over the Pacific Ocean.

She said the powerful natural climate phenomenon will lead to "more extreme storms in this country", and that households should stock up on food to be more resilient.

Her comments came as an National Audit Office (NAO) report warned Britain's food supply chain is vulnerable to plant or human disease outbreaks, cyber-attacks and extreme weather.

The NAO said the Department for Food, the Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra) had not done enough in recent years to improve supply chain resilience, and that UK households are less prepared for emergencies than those in several other countries such as Finland and Sweden.

The government launched its national security strategy last year, which warned that the UK must "actively prepare for the possibility of the UK coming under direct threat, potentially in a wartime scenario".

It said the nation was "in an era in which we face confrontation with those who are threatening security", and referred to Russia's war against Ukraine and "Iranian hostile activity on British soil".

The government said building national resilience meant reducing reliance on others and ensuring UK supply chains and energy security could be maintained "even in times of crisis".

stories.body:
Person named ‘K’ from China paid five defendants to injure Huang Yi-hao, New Taipei prosecutors say

Taiwanese prosecutors have charged five men over a plot to ram a car into a comedian who made fun of the Chinese Communist party and Xi Jinping .

Taiwan has repeatedly accused China of transnational repression to silence critics on the self-governed island, which Beijing claims as its territory and has vowed to take by force if necessary.

In one performance, Huang Yi-hao insulted the Chinese leader’s appearance, compared him to Winnie-the-Pooh and tore into his political record.

Prosecutors in New Taipei said on Wednesday that an individual from mainland China who was identified as “K” had paid the five defendants to injure Huang badly enough to require hospitalisation.

The prosecutors said: “This case involves a serious incident in which the Chinese Communist party is suspected of using cross-border suppression tactics to direct lawless elements in our country to suppress dissenting political voices through extreme violence.”

China’s Taiwan Affairs Office did not respond to requests for comment.

A GPS tracker was allegedly put on Huang’s scooter months before the attack to identify his daily routines, Taiwan’s Central News Agency said. On 11 September, two defendants drove into Huang’s bike as he rode home, but stopped after hearing Huang scream, prosecutors said.

The comedian was left with a bruised pelvis and the suspects then allegedly pretended to help with an insurance claim in order to send a photo of Huang’s medical certificate to K.

K refused to pay the full sum of NT$450,000 (US$13,900; £10,370) promised to the suspects because Huang’s injuries were only minor, the statement said.

On Wednesday, Huang reposted a video from December 2025 in which he asked the audience to help him by shouting out the name of the person he was about to describe.

In a fast-paced diatribe, the comedian, dressed in a traditional gown, evoked “swept-back hair” and a “plump figure”, and criticised policies on Hong Kong, Covid and the property market. After finishing with an expletive, the crowd chanted back Xi’s name before breaking into applause.

In May, two people were prosecuted after spreading faeces and paint at a Taipei club hours before a Huang show.

Lev Nachman, a professor of political science at National Taiwan University, said: “It is important to remember that what we are reading about is obviously a more extreme case, but there have been threats and acts of violence against critics of the Communist party here in Taiwan for many years.”

Taiwan’s Mainland Affairs Council said in October that at least 126 individuals had been affected by Chinese transnational repression.

The Guardian has contacted the Chinese foreign ministry for comment.

In a post on Wednesday, Huang said: “If people can be subjected to this kind of treatment simply for criticising the Chinese Communist party when it does not even govern Taiwan, how can we expect to retain our current freedom of speech if the CCP were ever to rule Taiwan?”

In another post on Facebook, Huang said he would not cancel future performances but that he was “no hero”.

“I write it because it’s funny,” he said. “If I stop, it will only be because I’ve got bored of it.”

stories.title: Introducing Our New Surveillance Self-Defense Guide: Online Privacy for Parents and Youth
stories.summary: The internet is a vast and confusing place no matter your age. Trying to help youth engage with it safely and privately is a complicated topic that touches on many different skillsets and ideas. But just because it’s complicated doesn’t mean it’s impossible. We’ve launched our Online Privacy for Parents and Youth Surveillance Self-Defense guide in hopes to provide a framework for finding solutions that work for you. EFF rolls out this crucial resource as state and local governments consider ill-advised laws that cut young people off from essential information and experiences. This particularly harms vulnerable youth and marginalized groups who often find safety in supportive online communities they can't access offline. Such laws also entail age gating, which compromises the privacy of all internet users and stifles young users’ ability to learn, grow , and express themselves . Young people have unique needs and those needs change over time. Trying to protect from everything all the time is an exhausting process, but the security community has long had a solution for this: security planning (also called threat modeling). The idea is to provide a series of questions designed to help you focus on what’s truly important. When it comes to online privacy, this is as applicable for youth and parents as it is for anyone else. We used a security plan as our foundation for this guide because deciding what is and isn’t important is the first step we should all take when assessing our privacy risks. But this isn’t a place for quick fixes, and every young person has their unique needs and considerations. There is no single tool or technology fix that can substitute for spending time learning, and then teaching a young person, how the internet works, how to use it, what sorts of harms exist, and how to navigate those harms. Solutions are rarely about the tools or software you use. It’s about understanding the threats and concerns you have, and then determining what steps you can take to mitigate those risks. We hope our Online Privacy for Parents and Youth guide can help provide the outline to get the conversation started. Donate Today!

stories.body:
Polls show US voters are deeply upset by high gas prices and are likely to punish Republicans in the midterms as a result

How will Trump’s mass deportation agenda shape the US midterm elections? Our reporters answer your questions

With fewer than two weeks until the midterm s, US voters are unlikely to see relief on one of this election cycle’s main issues: gas prices.

Airing up her car’s tires at a Speedway in Perrysburg, Ohio , Toledo resident Sharie Smith, 41, says soaring costs are having a direct impact on her life.

“It’s affecting my budget,” she says. “You got to take away certain things, you got to take away from your kids, like extracurricular activities.” She says high gas prices are making it harder to pay for the fees for her children’s football games.

Every 10 days, she used to fill up her gray Chevy Malibu for $30 to $40, but now it costs $50 to $60. It stings, she says. “Especially that with the price of groceries,” she adds.

“And I don’t even have a big car. I feel bad for those people with big cars, like trucks.”

Donald Trump has made many promises about bringing down gas prices and specifically touted several diesel cost-savings deals this month, but voters won’t see lower costs by 3 November, say energy analysts.

National average prices for gasoline and diesel are down marginally from a month ago, according to AAA , but remain substantially higher than last year. Compared with 2025, gasoline costs are up more than $1.25 a gallon, at $4.29, while diesel prices are up nearly 75%, to $6.30 a gallon.

Polls show that US voters are deeply upset by high gas prices and are likely to punish Republicans as a result. A 10 October poll by Politico showed that even if Trump were to bring the price of gasoline down by $1 a gallon, most voters polled would not likely be swayed to vote Republican.

Earlier this month, Trump announced several deals attempting to lower diesel prices, including promoting greater use of “red dye” diesel fuel normally reserved for off-highway use, temporarily lifting sanctions on Russian diesel imports, and now a one-time, $8bn diesel-fuel subsidy for farmers to help with harvest.

“Diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST! Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my greatest priority,” Trump posted on his social media site.

Ed Hirs, energy fellow at the University of Houston, says these moves will have no impact. “Zero. No elaboration needed,” he says.

Under the Russia deal, the US can import 2.24m barrels of Russian diesel, with more to follow. That initial figure amounts to just 14 hours of US diesel demand, says Andrew Critchlow, head of energy news for Dow Jones Energy. For context, the global diesel market uses nearly 30m barrels a day.

Hirs adds that the deal with Putin is not for new supply. “It was going someplace. It was going someplace at a discount. And now what Trump has done is, rather than have Russia sell it at a discount, they’re selling it for full value. He’s given them a huge windfall,” Hirs says.

Diesel fuel is an important transportation fuel globally, critical in the last-mile delivery of most consumer goods, so everyone feels the pinch, says Rob Thummel, senior portfolio manager at Tortoise Capital. Energy prices across the board are higher because of the US war on Iran, which closed the strait of Hormuz, through which much of the world’s crude oil flows.

Producing more diesel is difficult because Middle East refineries were damaged early in the war, and Chinese refiners are unable to get enough oil to produce any extra fuel for world markets. Recent attacks on Russian refiners by Ukrainian drones have further cut global supplies. US refineries have access to domestic oil but are running at maximum capacity, Thummel says.

The White House has characterized its recent executive order to temporarily allow greater use of red-dye diesel as a cost-saving measure for farmers and truckers. This fuel is exempt from federal excise taxes because it is intended for farmers and off-road machinery and is stained red to differentiate it from regular diesel. The White House says the 24.4 cents per gallon discount will save those drivers about $60 on a 250-gallon fill up.

Yet Hirs says it gives farmers more competition for fuel, which will raise their prices. Farmers already are being buffeted by higher operating costs across the board and losing China as a key export market because of the US’s trade war with the Asian nation.

Prices could rise as energy demand increases in the winter heating months, especially in places that use heating oil, experts add. Energy prices are seasonal, and prices are usually lower at this time of year since it’s neither cooling nor heating season, says Jay Hatfield, chief investment officer of real-asset investment firm InfraCap. Despite typically lower seasonal demand, prices are already high.

after newsletter promotion

There are risks of higher prices if the fighting in the Middle East escalates, Hatfield says, pointing to a pickup of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia as an example.

Critchlow says with many countries having depleted strategic stocks and few countries have released reserves, it might not take too much to push prices up. “I think that we are in a very fragile position now, marketwise,” he says.

The only moves that will lower energy costs are to open the strait of Hormuz to get more oil flowing, and to negotiate a peace accord between Russia and Ukraine, as these two conflicts are interlinked with energy markets, the energy experts say.

If those conflicts were resolved, Critchlow says the energy situation could be drastically different two years from now, with the world being oversupplied with fossil-fuel energy.

That change can’t come soon enough for some drivers. Lotanpa Jones, a home healthcare aide, was filling up at a Mobil in St Charles, Missouri, earlier this month. Regular fuel was $4.09 a gallon – last 1 October the national average price was $3.15 to $3.19, according to data from AAA . Diesel was $6.59 a gallon, up from $3.71 a year ago, according to data tracked by the US Energy Information Administration (EIA)

“I can tell you this is making me want to park my car,” said Jones.

She said she had last filled up her car two days earlier and now was adding another $55.

“It’s affecting a lot because you gotta decide what you’re gonna buy,” she said. “It’s major.”

Jones said she thought it would affect who people vote for. “Most definitely. Yes, this is extreme.”

Ironically, given Trump’s antipathy towards electric vehicles, Critchlow foresees the current crisis eventually pushing electrification for consumers, heavy industry and agriculture in the US. The shift in consumption and energy mix mirrors the 1970s energy shock, he says. “We are going to see something similar,” he says.

In the meantime, gas prices are likely to take their toll on Republicans come 3 November. Back in Ohio , Smith, a home health nurse, says she has already lost patients because of Medicaid eligibility changes made by the state, which she criticized Republicans for. “They’re thinking about the wrong things, and now the price of gas is going up,” Smith says.

As for who she is voting for, she says: “I’m going Democrat.” As for the Republican candidates, she adds: “They don’t have any idea what people are going through.”

stories.body:
Young people are facing a future that feels increasingly uncertain. Although every generation experiences turbulence while navigating adolescence, the pressures experienced by Gen Z – those born between 1997 and 2012 – are different and seem more pervasive.

From climate change and mental health concerns to academic pressure, housing costs, job and economic insecurity, today’s young people are navigating a complex set of expectations. Understanding their frustrations, including those expressed through protests across Europe, requires looking beyond individual experiences to the social conditions shaping their lives.

Adolescence has long been seen as a period of “storm and stress”. This reflecting a belief that is a universal and inevitable period of emotional turmoil, behavioural conflict and identity crisis. However, this has been increasingly challenged.

Rather than being defined solely by difficulty and disruption, adolescence is increasingly viewed as a period of possibility, opportunity and growth . Yet realising that potential depends heavily on the social environments in which young people grow up.

A growing body of evidence highlights adolescence as a critical developmental period with profound implications for future health and wellbeing. There is also increasing recognition that adolescence extends well beyond the teenage years and well into the twenties .

Growing up under pressure

Young people nowadays grow up under intense and often overlapping pressure, and today this is to a higher extent than generations before.

Evidence from the World Health Organization’s Health Behaviour in School-aged Children study suggests that school-related pressure increased between 2002 and 2022 across many countries.

In 2022 , among 15-year-old girls, almost two-thirds reported feeling pressured by schoolwork, compared with less than half of boys. The same research documented declines in perceived family and peer support. In other words, young people appear to be facing increasing demands while some of the social resources that help them cope with those demands are weakening.

Parental expectations and criticism have also intensified in many contexts. Success is increasingly framed as an individual responsibility, while educational pathways have become more competitive. At the same time, social media can amplify processes of social comparison, putting young people’s achievements, appearance and lifestyles under constant public scrutiny. For many, there is little respite from the pressure to perform.

Economic concerns add another level of pressure. Rising living costs, high tertiary education expanses and uncertainty about future employment rank among young people’s greatest worries . Across the EU, 40% are highly concerned by rising prices and the cost of living. In 2026, national surveys show that around 70% of Irish adolescents consider emigration for better life conditions. Over 20% of Dutch secondary school students are concerned whether they will ever be able to afford a home. A warming planet and an uncertain future Today’s young people are growing up amid an increasingly visible climate crisis. They hear repeated warnings about the short- and long-term consequences of climate change. Their generation will be disproportionally affected , and they know it. For some, this contributes to feelings of anxiety , worry, sadness, anger and helplessness about environmental degradation and the future. Concerns like this about a genuine global threat can be a rational and entirely understandable response. What can make these concerns particularly difficult is the perception that the decisions affecting young people’s future are often made without their meaningful involvement or consideration of their needs. This cycle of intergenerational injustice needs to be acknowledged and addressed. When people feel they have little influence on issues that will meaningfully shape their lives, this can lead to frustration. Evidence from many countries suggest that Gen Z are experiencing poorer mental health than previous generations. Although patterns vary across cultures and contexts, large scale studies point to increasing levels of emotional distress and psychological difficulties among young people. Public discussions often focus on explanations at an individual level: excessive screen time, reduced resilience and difficulties coping with everyday challenges. While these factors may play a role, they do not account for the whole story. Mental health is shaped by the interaction between individual experiences and wider social, economic and cultural environments in which people live. As such, the current rise in mental health difficulties should not be understood as a solely individual problem. Rather, it reflects a response to broader societal pressures that young people face as they move towards adulthood. Despite these challenges, it would be wrong to portray Gen Z as a generation defined only by anxiety or pessimism. Protests concerning housing, education, climate policy and economic inequality can express frustration, but they also demonstrate agency and a desire to influence decisions about the future. A 2025 survey of 6,703 young people across Europe found that 80% of young respondents in Germany considered EU membership a good thing, up from 65% in 2024. In France, the figure rose from 53% to 60%. The study also highlighted the importance young people attach to making the cost of living affordable. These findings challenge the assumption that today’s young generation is simply disengaged from society. Young people are not passive recipients of social pressures. They organise, question existing arrangements and seek alternatives. The difficulties facing Gen Z are not entirely new. What makes their experience distinctive is the combination of pressures and the uncertainty surrounding the transition to adulthood. Rather than asking whether today’s young people have it harder than previous generations, we should ask more productive questions: what kind of society are we asking them to navigate? And what can be done to make it healthier, fairer and more hopeful?

Old clothes are often altered or transformed into something new. Leftover crop stalks and leaves are turned into animal feed, compost, cooking fuel or biogas. It’s the opposite of a system where resources are extracted from nature and turned into goods that are sold, used and eventually thrown away. Our research found that circular economies aren’t happening everywhere. Thirty-four African countries have banned plastic bags to some degree. Rwanda, Ethiopia, Ghana, Nigeria, South Africa and Morocco have set up facilities to recycle e-waste (discarded electronic devices). They’ve also set up projects that turn waste into energy. Kenya has rules that make manufacturers responsible for collecting and recycling their products after people finish using them.

Read more: From trash to power: how to harness energy from Africa’s garbage dumps - and save billions in future damage

Somalia, Sudan and Congo , however, still depend heavily on a system in which products are made, used and discarded.

Africa’s circular economy has been discussed by governments, businesses, development agencies and international organisations as if it needs to be based on an imported model of formal waste-management systems and high-tech recycling.

Read more: West Africa’s plastic waste could be fuelling the economy instead of polluting the ocean: experts

These approaches may have a role, but repairers, reclaimers (also known as waste pickers), farmers and small businesses across Africa are already repairing, reusing, reselling, sharing, recovering materials and converting organic waste into productive resources.

In other words, circular practices are already embedded in everyday economic activity in African countries. The priority is therefore not to replace these practices. What’s needed is to recognise and improve them, and find ways to make them happen on a bigger scale. This means giving local businesses and communities the finance, infrastructure, skills and supportive policies they need to expand what is already working.

Progress is possible but uneven

Our research found that several African countries have introduced policies and initiatives supporting aspects of a circular economy. For example, Rwanda has acted against plastic pollution and developed facilities for processing electronic waste.

South Africa has come up with rules for producers of goods to help manage and pay for their products even after selling them. These rules compel producers to support collection, reuse and recycling. This keeps materials in circulation and reduces waste.

Read more: Ghana’s businesses don’t always need costly tech. How to build on what’s already been done

Kenya has taken significant measures against single use plastic bags. In Ghana , the National Plastic Action Partnership brings together government, business and civil society. Nigeria is developing a national circular economy roadmap. Nigerian groups like Wecyclers have connected informal collectors with recycling markets.

Greater opportunities exist across agriculture and food systems , manufacturing , energy, and water and sanitation .

However, a policy on paper does not automatically produce an effective system. Waste collection remains inadequate in many African cities. There aren’t many recycling facilities on the continent. Local authorities often lack the funds, equipment and technical capacity to enforce regulations. Political instability and unreliable electricity supplies can make long term investment in circular economy projects difficult.

What needs to happen next

Africa’s move towards a circular economy must start with the basics: collecting waste, sorting it properly and disposing of it safely. As our research found, expensive technologies will not work well if waste is never collected or is too contaminated to recycle.

The African Union’s Continental Circular Economy Action Plan has some useful ideas on this. But its success will depend on how well it is put into practice in local communities. For many countries, improving everyday waste services should come before investing in high-tech solutions.

Read more: How the plastics industry shifted responsibility for recycling onto you, the consumer

Informal workers including reclaimers, repairers and second-hand traders are already central to Africa’s circular economy. They should be supported by governments. They need training, safer working conditions, facilities to work in, fair compensation and social protection. Including these workers in formal circular economy systems, while protecting their livelihoods, can help build a more inclusive and effective circular economy.

The success of circular economy policies should be judged on more than how much waste is kept out of rubbish dumps. Policymakers need to make sure that people benefit from the circular economy. Working conditions of recyclers should improve, recovered products must be affordable and local recycling enterprises must remain viable.

Read more: The circular economy may not be taking off: Here are six ways stakeholders can make it happen

Africa’s circular economy will emerge strongly if governments, businesses, communities, researchers and informal workers work together. The foundations of a circular economy already exist. African countries have a strong culture of repairing and reusing goods. Local experts and entrepreneurs who turn discarded materials into value are valued. The task now is to support these efforts without destroying the social and economic systems that sustain them.

stories.title: Nuclear Weapons Waste Made Workers Sick. Despite a Law Meant to Help, the DOE Keeps Fighting Their Claims.

stories.body:
Co-published with Cascade PBS and KUOW

Reporting Highlights

Toxic Legacy: Workers got sick cleaning up radioactive waste at a former federal nuclear weapons site in Washington, and the state passed a law to make it easier to claim benefits.

Litigating Workers’ Claims: The Department of Energy denies responsibility and has filed more than 500 legal appeals seeking to block state benefits being given to workers and their survivors.

Millions Go to Lawyers: DOE has spent nearly $12 million on outside lawyers and expert testimony to fight state compensation claims.

These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.

Lonnie Rouse shuffled into a wood-paneled conference room at the Washington state Capitol in March 2018. It had been nearly a decade since medical experts diagnosed him with a neurological disease they attributed to his exposure to chemicals at work. In the time since, he had acquired a stutter, begun limping and lost several teeth biting into a banana.

For nearly 20 years, Rouse had packaged plutonium and monitored radioactive waste at the Hanford Site , a now-decommissioned Department of Energy nuclear weapons production plant in south-central Washington and one of the most contaminated nuclear sites in the country. Tanks full of radioactive sludge exposed him to at least 48 potentially hazardous chemicals . The worksite was so toxic, he said, that the floor once melted the rubber off his boots.

Rouse was among the thousands of workers responsible for the ongoing environmental cleanup at Hanford, which has been underway since the DOE shut down the last reactor in the late 1980s. Congress has acknowledged , based on voluminous studies, that radiation at DOE sites poses health risks to workers.

Over time, some people at Hanford became so sick they could no longer work. Like Rouse, they filed for workers’ compensation. The DOE consistently challenged their claims and tried to shift the blame onto the workers themselves.

By the time Rouse took his place behind then-Gov. Jay Inslee, he was desperate. His 2009 workers’ compensation claim had been denied. He had burned through his retirement savings and declared bankruptcy.

As he watched, the governor signed a bill that was supposed to change his life.

For years, Hanford employees filing workers’ compensation claims had to prove the chemicals they were exposed to on the job made them sick. The new law Inslee signed flipped that burden of proof. Under the law , agencies were instructed to presume that working at Hanford had caused certain cancers, neurological diseases and respiratory illnesses . Now the Department of Energy would have to prove to the state that something other than the job had made the workers sick if it wanted to deny their claims.

Rouse thought the presumption law would speed up his claim for benefits. State lawmakers and the former governor thought it would force the DOE to take responsibility for the harm Hanford workers were experiencing.

But despite the law, the DOE continues to fight new and existing claims, Cascade PBS and ProPublica found. We asked the state for claims records going back to the presumption law’s passage in 2018, but the state only provided records going back three and a half years, to 2023. In that period, workers filed 102 new claims for benefits, state data shows. The DOE did not recommend approving a single one.

The state, which has final say, overruled the DOE and approved 75% of those claims. The DOE appealed all but seven of those approvals.

Cascade PBS and ProPublica spoke to workers, surviving family members, lawyers representing workers and state officials. They all pointed to a pattern: The DOE systematically challenges and then drags out workers’ compensation claims for years with recommended denials and subsequent legal appeals. Along the way, it has spent millions on outside lawyers and expert testimony, including doctor evaluations that point to other causes for workers’ illnesses.

The DOE has paid out benefits to Hanford workers in some cases, lawyers and families said, but it has done so while still actively appealing the claims. It warns workers that they may have to pay the money back.

Our reporting found that not even death ends the cycle of appeals. About 152 workers’ claims remain stranded in this legal limbo — approved by the state but still under appeal by the DOE. Half of those workers are dead. The DOE continues to fight to deny their families survivors’ benefits.

“It seems pretty coldhearted, calculated, that they’re trying to save money on the back of sick workers who they made sick,” said Gerry Pollet, one of the Washington state representatives who sponsored the 2018 presumption law, who is also a co-founder of the Hanford cleanup watchdog group Heart of America Northwest. “That’s why we needed a state law.”

After Cascade PBS and ProPublica raised questions about the DOE’s pattern of litigating claims, regulators at the Washington State Department of Labor and Industries met twice with DOE staff, state agency spokesperson Carrie McCausland said. But she could not point to any other actions the agency has taken beyond the two meetings.

“Agency staff are concerned and are right now assessing the severity of patterns we’ve seen,” McCausland wrote in an email.

The DOE did not answer detailed questions or respond to the newsrooms’ findings. In a statement, a spokesperson wrote that the DOE is following “all applicable local, state, and federal laws” and “has a long and successful record of accomplishment of protecting human health and the environment.”

The DOE has the right to file multiple appeals against a claim. According to court records, its appeals have sought to overturn claims approved by the state, narrow the period of back wages, or block survivors’ benefits, among other things. In appeals filings, the DOE’s lawyers have argued that factors other than work at Hanford played a role in the workers’ illnesses, including smoking, drinking, obesity or genetics.

In Rouse’s case, the energy department blamed alcoholism and family conflicts. The state agency that handles appeals did not find those arguments persuasive. DOE awarded Rouse most of his back pay in 2024, his lawyer said. Rouse declined to say how much that was, but said he is not touching the money until the legal process concludes.

In the nearly eight years it has been fighting his claim, the DOE has filed more than 20 appeals contesting different aspects of his claim.

“We were always told that nothing is out here that’s going to harm you — you do what you are supposed to do, and you do what you are trained to do, and you’re going to be fine,” said Rouse, who now receives 24-hour care.

“But that’s not what happens.”

“Depleted and Disgusted”

The smell of ammonia serves as a warning, workers say, that the underground tanks holding a mix of radioactive sludge have burped chemical vapors into the air above. From 1998 to 2008, it was Rouse’s job to monitor the toxic waste held in the “tank farms.” The containers together hold more than 50 million gallons of liquid waste. Rouse says he lost count of how many times tanks released toxic vapor that took his breath away, sometimes knocking him to the ground and making him vomit and bleed from his nose. According to a 2014 report funded by the federal government, tank farm workers exposed to chemical vapors commonly reported nausea, headaches and nosebleeds.

The liquid sloshing around in those tanks represented the radioactive byproducts of the Cold War. Hanford produced two-thirds of the plutonium for the nation’s nuclear arsenal and fueled the atomic bomb dropped on Nagasaki, Japan, in 1945.

The end of production in the late 1980s launched a cleanup effort that is expected to continue until at least 2086. As of January 2025, more than 13,000 people were working at Hanford, nearly all of them for private companies contracted by the DOE. It is one of the largest and most expensive efforts to remediate toxic waste in the nation’s history.

In 2000, Congress passed the Energy Employees Occupational Illness Compensation Program Act , which provides medical care and one-time payouts to workers at DOE sites across the country. It was an acknowledgement that the nation’s nuclear weapons workers had been exposed to radioactive substances known to cause cancer. In it, lawmakers referred to a DOE policy “to litigate occupational illness claims, which has deterred workers from filing workers’ compensation claims and has imposed major financial burdens for such employees who have sought compensation.”

But the benefits of the federal program were limited: It capped payouts at $400,000.

Washington’s workers’ compensation system, by contrast, can provide steady wage replacement or a pension benefit, in some cases, for the rest of an injured employee’s life. It’s a program that can easily surpass the maximum federal benefit.

The state went further with its 2018 presumption law. Such laws generally protect firefighters who are regularly exposed to smoke, burned plastics and extreme heat. The National Council on Compensation Insurance, the Washington state attorney general and Pollet all said they were unaware of any other state that has extended that protection for radiological workers.

The federal government challenged Washington’s state law later that year in court, arguing it was discriminatory because it only applied to Hanford and the DOE.

Anticipating a Supreme Court decision that ultimately agreed, lawmakers passed an expanded version that covered all workers at “radiological hazardous waste facilities” in the state, including the state’s only functioning nuclear power plant and a French-owned facility that manufactures nuclear fuel rods. Nonetheless, roughly 75% of the 428 claims filed since 2018 have come from the DOE’s Hanford workers, according to the state Department of Labor and Industries.

Kathleen Kersey spent 10 years at Hanford, during both the production and cleanup stages. Much of her work involved measuring radiation around the site and making sure levels were safe. She says her safety training covered radiation, but not other hazards like chemical vapors burping from the waste tanks.

Kersey struggles to walk, has short-term memory problems and at one point lost vision in her right eye for three months. A doctor diagnosed her with multiple sclerosis, which is a neurological disorder, one of the categories of illnesses the state’s presumption law recognizes as related to chemical exposure at Hanford. In 2019 she filed a claim, which the state approved.

The DOE has appealed, arguing that something other than her time at Hanford caused her multiple sclerosis.

Kersey is one of the 152 workers still awaiting a resolution on her workers’ compensation claim. The DOE has not paid her any back wages, she said. The DOE declined to comment on her case.

“I feel depleted and disgusted,” Kersey said of the appeals process. “It makes me feel like I’m worthless. I have no value.”

“When Does This End?”

State records show that the DOE has filed more than 500 appeals since the presumption law passed in 2018. In 20 cases, as it did with Rouse, the DOE has appealed a single worker’s claim half a dozen times or more.

“We have seen tremendous pushback from DOE on essentially almost every single case that’s been brought,” said Washington State Attorney General Nick Brown.

Rouse’s wife, Melinda, said she knew something was wrong when he could not remember how to cut an orange. His vision started to blur, he stumbled often, and suddenly he felt irritable all the time. His primary care physician first thought he might have had a brain tumor. The physician referred him to a neurologist who noted cognitive impairment, possibly due to exposure to multiple toxins at the Hanford Site. The neurologist then referred him to a neuropsychologist, who diagnosed him with “toxic encephalopathy” in 2009, saying it was “more likely than not” that chemical exposure damaged his brain, according to court records.

The U.S. Department of Labor agreed too, approving him in 2010 for benefits under the Energy Employees Occupational Illness Compensation Program Act, saying it was “at least as likely as not” that Hanford contributed to his illness. A federal medical consultant even praised the neuropsychologist who assessed Rouse for his “unusually thorough analysis of causation.”

Rouse refiled his 2009 state workers’ compensation claim under the new law in 2018. Washington state approved it later that year.

The DOE appealed. It hired a medical toxicologist, who reviewed Rouse’s medical records and testified that he did not have the disease he claimed, and brought in an industrial hygienist, who downplayed the exposure risks at Hanford. The DOE’s toxicologist testified that Rouse’s drinking was “the most significant, what we might term, ‘toxic exposure’ that’s described in the medical record.”

A group of three physicians and an industrial hygienist have collectively earned over $1.7 million testifying against Hanford workers since the presumption law’s passage, according to DOE invoices the newsrooms obtained by a federal records request. One of the DOE’s go-to expert witness doctors earned more than $200,000 from the DOE last year alone. He did not respond to multiple emails seeking comment.

A single law firm, Wallace, Mann, Capener, Bishop & Debney, handles all of the DOE’s appeals. In addition to the fees paid to expert witnesses, the department paid the firm nearly $10 million between 2018 and 2025. The law firm did not reply to multiple requests for comment.

In cases where the DOE has appealed the state’s approval of a claim since 2018, the agency that handles appeals has sided with workers nearly 9 times out of 10, according to state data.

Pollet, the state representative who sponsored the 2018 presumption bill, acknowledged that the law has fallen short of his expectation.

“This was supposed to have ended a decade ago,” he said about sick Hanford workers still awaiting back wages and medical care. “It’s even worse than it was 10 years ago.”

“I think their actions are not only despicable, but they are criminal,” he said of the DOE.

The state Department of Labor and Industries said it expected “to engage further with the DOE,” which could include putting the department on an improvement plan and monitoring its progress.

Another option state regulators have is to revoke the DOE’s ability to accept and pay out claims directly. According to the state Department of Labor and Industries, the contractors that employ Hanford workers on behalf of the DOE would then decide whether to join the state-managed fund or seek state approval to manage claims themselves. Doing so could limit the DOE’s power to appeal, but contractors would still have that right.

Brown, the state attorney general, said he wants to wait and see how the DOE’s appeals of claims play out in higher courts. He hopes that once the DOE’s losses start stacking up, it will slow the volume of its litigation.

Attorney Charlynn Hull said she thought the DOE’s approach might soften during the Biden administration. But Hull said she observed no change in the DOE’s behavior. Her firm, Smart Law, represents the majority of Hanford workers’ compensation claimants, including Rouse and Kersey.

One of the hardest things about the DOE’s appeals, Hull said, is the testifying that the children and spouses of dead workers must do.

“I think that it’s just, it’s tormenting to them, in many ways, to relive how awful that experience was, especially with the cancer-related death,” Hull said. “When does this end?”

Dying While Under Appeal

For Isidoro Mata Jr., it ended with his children draining fluid from his lungs through a tube doctors had surgically inserted into his chest.

Mata demolished buildings at Hanford for nearly 30 years. Court records show he was diagnosed in 2015 with thyroid cancer, one of the illnesses that Washington’s law ties to work at Hanford. Sara Chilcoat, his daughter, said he kept working as long as he could.

State claims managers approved Mata’s claim in 2019. The DOE appealed, arguing that “medical opinion supports denial of this claim as not related to the distinctive conditions of employment.” The appeal did not elaborate further. The state forced the DOE to pay his wages and the cost of his medications, Chilcoat said. But the DOE filed a separate motion to stop his benefits while the appeal was adjudicated.

In its motion, the DOE argued that it was likely to prevail in its appeal because a doctor who examined Mata in 2019 believed his cancer was unrelated to his work at Hanford, according to court records. The state found the doctor’s examination “lacking in objective findings.”

“He was fighting for his life while they were trying to do that,” Chilcoat said. “That makes me mad.”

Mata’s case file notes that he missed three meetings with DOE lawyers in 2020. The state attorney general’s office sent the appeals judge a letter in July explaining that Mata was unable to participate because of his chemotherapy treatments. The DOE, which did not respond to questions about Mata’s case, dropped its appeal in December.

Less than three months later, Mata died.
