Reporting Highlights

Rural Cuts: Delays resulting from the U.S. Postal Service’s cost-cutting measures have endangered the validity of ballots cast in rural areas, a ProPublica analysis found.

Rejected Ballots: The rates of ballots rejected for arriving late this year doubled or tripled in areas affected by the cuts compared to the 2022 primary. That wasn’t the case elsewhere.

Extraordinary Measures: Postal Service leaders say special procedures in place for the Nov. 3 election should prevent similar delays, but experts warn that mistakes are likely.

These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.

In early August, election workers north of Spokane, Washington, went across the street to the post office to check for late mail-in ballots. It was three days after the primary and they were expecting no more than a few dozen.

Instead, their mailbox was brimming with envelopes — more than 500 of them, each a vote that wouldn’t count. The sight was “jarring,” said Auditor Lori Larsen, a Republican who oversees voting in Stevens County.

Across the region, other election officials were getting similar jolts. In the 11 predominately rural counties in eastern Washington, nearly 2,000 ballots came in late, compared to about 600 in 2022, the previous midterm primary.

In recent weeks, concerns about mail-in voting disruptions have focused almost entirely on President Donald Trump’s now-shelved plan to sharply restrict who can vote by mail .

But a ProPublica data analysis shows that delays resulting from the U.S. Postal Service’s cost-cutting measures have endangered the validity of ballots cast in rural areas, not only in Washington, but across the country.

Over the past three years, as mail volume continued to plummet and annual deficits ballooned, the Postal Service started consolidating the processing of first-class mail at larger regional plants instead of at smaller hubs closer to local post offices. Then, in a little-noted switch that mostly took effect after the 2024 election, the agency cut the frequency of mail pickups in half at many post offices 50 miles or more from these processing plants, from twice daily to once.

The changes often added a day or more to delivery time and, most importantly for ballots, pushed back postmarking, which doesn’t happen until mail reaches the regional centers.

In this year’s primary, the effects of the cuts were clearest in five states that make detailed data on mail-in ballots available: Washington, California, Ohio, North Carolina and Oregon. All have or recently had grace periods allowing ballots to count if they come in after Election Day as long as they’re postmarked by the deadline.

In these states, the number of ballots rejected for arriving late soared in counties affected by the service changes compared to 2022, ProPublica’s analysis showed.

Rejection rates in counties where services were cut doubled or tripled from what they were four years ago, dwarfing any increases in counties where postal pickups remained as they were, our analysis showed. In urban Spokane, for example, the number of ballots rejected for being late actually dropped this year.

Across the five states, the delays have had the most substantial effect in areas that voted for Trump in 2024, ProPublica’s analysis shows. In Washington, Secretary of State Steve Hobbs, a Democrat, said he sees the service changes directed by Republican appointees leading the Postal Service as a way to undermine mail-in voting.

“I don’t think they realized how much it was going to affect their voter base,” he said, adding that Washington has “a lot of rural Republican voters.”

Rates of Rejection Due to Late Ballots Were Higher in Counties with Reduced Mail Service

Postal Service leaders say such delays are less likely in the Nov. 3 general election because of “extraordinary measures” the agency puts into place for these votes, when there’s typically far more turnout. They have circulated a memo to the nation’s more than 30,000 post offices saying that for the 10 days before the election, managers should separate completed ballots from other first-class mail and deliver those intended for local election offices the day they come in.

At an Oct. 15 news conference, Postal Service leaders emphasized the agency’s longstanding recommendation that voters mail ballots back at least a week before their states’ deadlines, while defending the agency’s ability to fast-track ballots through the system.

“We work to identify and address issues quickly,” said Amber McReynolds, chair of the Postal Service board of governors, “so ballots can continue to move swiftly from election offices to voters and from voters back to election offices.”

Election consultants, researchers and former Postal Service officials told ProPublica that the guidance for the upcoming vote gave more detailed directions on how to expedite ballots. They said they hoped the agency’s special measures would limit delays, but some said mistakes were likely.

“I don’t think we can say with any kind of conviction that there will be no ballots rejected,” said Tammy Patrick, chief programs officer of the National Association of Election Officials. “It isn’t a question of ‘if,’ but a question of ‘how many.'”

A pilot program instituting the delivery changes in 18 regions before the 2024 election ran into problems. An audit by the Postal Service’s inspector general found that agency staff in these areas sometimes didn’t handle ballots correctly, mainly because instructions weren’t clearly communicated. (A Postal Service spokesperson said “learnings from the pilot” have been applied as the program has expanded.)

After this year’s primary, reports by media outlets noted that mail-in ballot rejection rates were higher than in the past, but ProPublica’s analysis shows these increases were directly connected to Postal Service changes. Research published in September by the Brookings Institution also found this connection, projecting that if the pattern held in the general election, tens of thousands of mail-in ballots could be rejected.

At least seven closely contested congressional districts — including Washington’s 3rd, California’s 22nd and North Carolina’s 11th — are in areas that were affected by service changes in the primary, ProPublica found.

Elena Patel, who conducted the Brookings analysis, said service changes may still imperil mail-in votes in the general election.

“I think there remain risks to ballots,” she said, adding that the Postal Service’s plan for the general election “depends on flawless execution.”

Mail-in voting has become more popular over the last decade, with many states broadening access to it during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Nearly 1 in 3 Americans voted this way in 2022 and 2024. Trump himself frequently votes by mail, and in recent weeks has started to encourage his supporters to do so as well, though he has claimed without evidence that the process is rife with fraud.

The Postal Service has mostly ensured the timely delivery of hundreds of millions of ballots , even as mail volume overall has dropped 50% from its high in 2006 .

When Louis DeJoy was appointed postmaster general in spring 2020, he inherited an $81 billion operating deficit and rapidly took steps such as eliminating overtime to reduce costs, under pressure from Trump and others in his administration . (DeJoy did not respond to questions from ProPublica.)

The NAACP sued that August, alleging the measures could affect mail-in votes in that year’s general election. Courts ordered DeJoy to reverse some of the cuts and the Postal Service agreed to implement special procedures to ensure ballots weren’t delayed. The Postal Service has continued following those procedures since.

Still, DeJoy went forward with a 10-year restructuring plan designed to save the agency billions. It ended evening pickups from some post offices, often in rural areas. Trucks serving these places travel long distances and at times were mostly empty. This part of the plan — called regional transportation optimization, or RTO — was projected to eventually save the Postal Service $4 billion a year.

The agency announced the national rollout of the RTO plan in 2024, but DeJoy agreed to pause it leading up to that year’s November election, leaving only about 4,000 ZIP codes in the pilot project affected by the service changes.

Mail Services Have Been Cut in 16,000 More ZIP Codes Since the 2024 Election

A pilot program that reduced mail pickups to save money was paused in the lead-up to the 2024 election. The rollout has since resumed, and the changes have been made in five times as many ZIP codes for the 2026 midterms.

In January 2025, the Postal Regulatory Commission, which oversees the Postal Service, warned that moving forward with the plan would be disruptive to rural communities and might not save as much money as expected. The Postal Service rolled out the reductions anyway, extending the changes to almost 20,000 ZIP codes to date. Officials said they expect the system to be fully implemented within two years.

This January, the agency put out a statement saying the transportation cuts would mean it took longer for mail, including ballots, to be postmarked and delivered. But the Postal Service didn’t specify which voters would be affected by the slowdowns and which wouldn’t.

A plan to reduce mail pickup frequency is being rolled out in ZIP codes that are more than 50 miles from a sorting facility. Areas not subject to the plan are mostly in or near large cities.

Though the delay from RTO is often only a day, mail can be delayed longer if it’s deposited in a mailbox after the daily pickup time, or just before Sunday or a holiday.

A Postal Service spokesperson said the agency told election officials that RTO would change schedules and reemphasized the need for voters to get their ballots in the mail at least a week ahead of time. Election officials in Washington said the Postal Service wasn’t direct enough about the fact that the changes would lead to delays in delivering and postmarking ballots.

“What they said was, ‘We are going to change the way we do postmarks,'” said Hobbs, Washington’s secretary of state. “That was it.”

Patel, the Brookings analyst and a former Postal Regulatory Commission employee, said that more direct communication to voters could have helped change their behavior. “That’s the part that I think has not been super transparent about the whole process,” she said.

Many of the areas that saw a spike in late ballots were in Western states, which were the earliest and most enthusiastic adopters of expanded mail-in voting.

In 2004, Washington became the second state to start conducting all-mail elections, in which every eligible voter automatically receives a mail-in ballot. Most residents vote by putting their ballots in drop boxes. Still, in 2024, about 33% put them in the mail.

In the 30 mostly rural Washington counties most affected by RTO, the percentage of ballots postmarked late more than tripled compared to the 2022 primary, ProPublica found.

Has Mail Service Been Reduced in Your ZIP Code?

If the frequency of mail pickups has been reduced in your area, mail may take longer to send and receive, and the date on the postmark could be later than the day you dropped it off, which may matter for mail like ballots that is subject to a deadline.

In Garfield County, in southeastern Washington, 19 ballots — nearly 1 in 10 cast — had late postmarks this year. In 2022, only a single ballot was postmarked late. In Pend Oreille County, in northeast Washington along the Idaho panhandle, 6% of ballots were rejected for arriving late, compared to 1% in the 2022 primary.

“It was pretty awful telling people we couldn’t count their votes,” said Marianne Nichols, Pend Oreille’s longtime auditor. “They were quite upset because they felt like, ‘Why? This was in the mailbox on election day, the post office picked it up and had it.’ They felt like it should have counted.”

In Stevens County, the percentage of ballots rejected for having a late postmark jumped to 8%, from 1% in 2022.

Steve Hutkins, a retired professor who analyzes the effect of Postal Service changes on Savethepostoffice.com, also found that places in Washington with RTO had more ballot rejections during local elections earlier this year for school board and other measures. The patterns “set off the alarm bells,” he said.

Stuart Holmes, the state’s director of elections, said he reached out to Postal Service officials to find out what had happened, but got few answers and no specifics on delays related to RTO, which were a “total surprise,” he said.

Election officials in California and Oregon also reported thousands more ballots rejected for arriving late during their primaries. Counties affected by RTO, including Kern County, California, had substantially higher rates of ballots rejected for mail-related reasons, ProPublica found.

Kern County’s assistant registrar of voters, Laura Cantu, said election officials are urging rural voters to use drop boxes to cast their ballots in the general election.

The expansion of RTO had a similar effect in North Carolina and Ohio, where the rates of late ballots were about twice as high in counties affected by the restructuring as rates in counties that weren’t. Since 2022, these states have also eliminated grace periods in which ballots postmarked by Election Day could count even if they arrived later. Voters unused to the tighter deadlines also could have contributed to an increase in late ballots.

ProPublica didn’t find any association between RTO and higher rates of late ballots in Wisconsin, even though clerks reported delays involving mail-in ballots cast in its state election, held this spring. (Other Postal Service changes may have contributed to the delays.)

Wisconsin’s data does not distinguish ballots sent by mail from those cast in drop boxes or in person, making it impossible to definitively measure rejection rates just for ballots returned by mail. Election researchers said Wisconsin’s deadline for mail ballots, which must come into election offices by 8 p.m. on Election Day, also probably had an effect.

“If you know that you don’t have a grace period, it probably affects voter behavior,” said Patel, the Brookings researcher.

Recent Postal Service audits have found that RTO-related changes had saved the agency about $2.8 billion by the end of fiscal year 2025 — less money than expected — and are slowing down all first-class mail, not just ballots. Residents of rural areas are waiting longer for everything from prescriptions to bills, a report published in September by the Postal Service’s inspector general said.

A Postal Service spokesperson still defended the plan, both for financial reasons and to adjust to the changing marketplace. “These savings are both significant and necessary,” he said.

In the lead-up to Nov. 3, the agency’s plan is to route ballots meant for local election offices to a nearby postal facility or directly to their destination. They shouldn’t go to regional plants, which the Postal Service says should minimize delays.

Larsen, the Stevens County auditor, is encouraging Washington voters to deposit their ballots in drop boxes rather than relying on the mail. Since the primary, she’s increased the number of red, white and blue drop boxes that sit outside government buildings from seven to 12. Near each box, there’s a large sign encouraging people to take selfies when they vote and send the photos to Larsen.

In prior years, Larsen said, she avoided telling voters how or when to vote, concerned they might regret choices they made if critical information later emerged about the candidates. That’s no longer uppermost in her mind.

“Now we are more concerned that we get your ballot,” she said.

stories.title: Arms Control, not Ukraine, Should Be on the Superpower Agenda
stories.summary: The proposed meeting of Trump, Putin, and Xi nex month in Shenzhen could make real progress on arms control—as long as it steers clear of the Ukraine war. The post Arms Control, not Ukraine, Should Be on the Superpower Agenda appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Shutterstock

Asked at the White House whether he would sit down with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping on the sidelines of next month’s APEC summit in Shenzhen, Donald Trump steered the conversation from Ukraine to warheads. “We would have it to talk about nuclear weapons and denuclearization,” he said. Russia, he added, “has been fine on Ukraine.” In the same exchange he suggested it was time for someone other than Volodymyr Zelensky to negotiate for Kyiv.

Two proposals now ride on one invitation. Putin, according to The Wall Street Journal , pitched the meeting as a way to end the war on terms that favor Moscow. Trump pitched it as arms control. Only one of them belongs in Shenzhen.

The summit itself is worth holding. The two largest nuclear arsenals have gone more than eight months without a single binding limit since New START expired on February 5. Trump turned down Putin’s offer to observe its ceilings voluntarily for another year, saying he wanted a better treaty. He has no better treaty. He has a venue.

The objection is easy to predict: China will refuse to play. Beijing’s foreign ministry spokeswoman, Mao Ning , said last week that asking China to join trilateral disarmament talks “at this stage” is “neither fair, reasonable nor realistic,” and that the United States carries “special and primary responsibility.” In Washington, that line will be interpreted as obstruction.

Read the numbers before reading the motive. SIPRI’s latest yearbook puts the U.S. military stockpile at 3,700 warheads and Russia’s at 4,400. China holds about 620 . Even if Beijing passes 1,000 by 2030, SIPRI notes, it would have about a quarter of either arsenal. Russia and the United States control roughly 83 percent of the world’s usable warheads.

A negotiation that asks the smallest of the three to freeze first is not arms control. It asks China to accept permanent inferiority as the entry fee. When Washington and Moscow signed SALT I in 1972, nobody asked Britain, France, or China to sign too.

However, China’s arsenal is growing faster than anyone’s. SIPRI estimates that Beijing may now have around 34 warheads deployed with operational forces, up from 24, and it has loaded missiles into three new silo fields. Washington’s worry is not invented.

Three things could come out of that room that none of the three leaders would have to sell at home as a defeat.

The first would be a restored ceiling. Washington and Moscow can announce that they will observe New START’s central limit of 1,550 deployed strategic warheads for 12 months and resume data exchanges. Russia has already said that it would keep to those limits if the United States does. The pledge costs Trump nothing, and the Arms Control Association has suggested the three leaders could reaffirm their test-ban commitments in the same statement.

Second, China could offer something that corresponds to the size of its arsenal. Beijing has held to a no-first-use pledge since its first test in 1964 and has pressed the other nuclear powers for years to adopt one as well. A three-way reaffirmation of the January 2022 statement by the five nuclear powers that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought, paired with a leaders’ hotline and missile-launch notifications among the three, would bring China into a risk-reduction process without asking it to cap an arsenal that’s a fraction of the others. That is a track Beijing can accept, and the host of the summit has every reason to want it to work.

Third, the leaders could agree to a written firewall. The communiqué should state plainly that Ukrainian territory is not on the Shenzhen agenda. Here Beijing’s own record helps. China’s February 2023 position paper on the war opened with respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of all countries. On Monday, Mao Ning said that the ministry had no information about any trilateral meeting. Beijing has shown no appetite for hosting the carve-up of a third country, and it has every interest in a Shenzhen summit remembered for warheads rather than borders.

The firewall matters because the alternative is already visible. Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha , warned that a meeting of the three without Kyiv would “encourage Putin to continue this war.” The day after Trump called Russia “fine,” a Russian drone strike near the Kyiv-Odesa highway killed three people . The Washington Post reported that the administration has not approved the interceptors Kyiv needs.

A summit that swaps arms control for Ukrainian land would hand Putin the prize his army has failed to take, and it would discredit the nuclear track for a generation.

From Karachi, the picture is less abstract. The big three are not the only problem. SIPRI counts India at 190 warheads and Pakistan at about 170 , and in May 2025 the two traded missile and drone strikes in the heaviest fire between nuclear-armed neighbors in decades. A Shenzhen deal will freeze nothing below the top tier. It would at least show that great powers can still sign something. South Asia has not seen such an example in a long time.

Trump likes to say he ends wars. He has a better chance of ending an arms race that has run without rules since February, and he can do it in a city whose host wants the meeting to succeed.

The test will be visible when APEC closes on November 19 . If the Shenzhen statement carries the number 1,550, the summit will have done what no arms control meeting has managed in five years. If it carries the word Ukraine without a Ukrainian in the room, it will be remembered as Yalta with a nuclear footnote.

stories.title: What Is Driving the Global Resurgence of Mangrove Forests?
stories.summary: After decades of losses, mangrove trees are gaining ground on coastlines around the world, often in places they have never grown before. Paradoxically, scientists say, warming temperatures and the destruction of inland forests are helping to power the revival. Read more on E360 →
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Mangroves on the island of Mauritius in the Indian Ocean. Adam Burton

ANALYSIS

After decades of losses, mangrove trees are gaining ground on coastlines around the world, often in places they have never grown before. Paradoxically, scientists say, warming temperatures and the destruction of inland forests are helping to power the revival.

By Fred Pearce • October 22, 2026

Facebook

Twitter

LinkedIn

Email

From the bayous of Louisiana to the backwaters of the Irrawaddy in Myanmar, from the lagoons of West Africa to the billabongs of northern Australia, mangroves are making a dramatic and unexpected comeback.

What a difference a couple of decades can make.

In 2007, ecologists from six countries asked in a letter published in the journal Science whether we would soon be living in “a world without mangroves.” One of the world’s most distinctive, biodiverse, and carbon-rich ecosystems was in rapid retreat in the face of encroaching agriculture, construction of sea walls, ports, and marinas, and rising sea levels. The mangroves seemed doomed.

But in recent months two separate studies have painted a very different picture. A high-resolution analysis of satellite imagery published in Science in June found that the stunted, salt-tolerant trees are now undergoing an “unexpected expansion,” healing after decades of destruction.

At the same time, a report on the State of the World’s Mangroves , published in September by a group of NGOs under the umbrella of the Global Mangrove Alliance, found that “mangroves are now increasing in extent, year on year,” said coauthor Mark Spalding of The Nature Conservancy.

For the first time, mangrove forests are expanding faster than they are declining, says a coastal ecologist.

It’s not that the destruction of mangroves has ended. But the Science study finds that new mangrove growth between 2010 and 2023 covered approximately 3,200 square miles, outpacing losses of around 2,400 square miles. Worldwide, mangrove cover is now back to the levels last seen in the 1980s.

The new findings are the surprising outcome of the most detailed analysis yet attempted of satellite imagery of mangroves over the past four decades, says Pete Bunting, a remote sensing analyst at Aberystwyth University in Wales, who worked on both studies. It shows that previous assessments had provided “a substantial underestimation of mangrove gains” over the past 15 years, says the Science study’s lead author Zhen Zhang of Tulane University in Louisiana.

“For the first time, these unique ecosystems are expanding at a faster rate than they are declining,” says Catherine Lovelock, a coastal ecologist at the University of Queensland, who was not involved in either study.

However, not all ecologists are celebrating.

For one thing, mangroves are recovering in some places thanks to environmental degradation elsewhere. For another, says Norman Duke, an ecologist at James Cook University in Queensland, Australia, and lead author of the 2007 letter, mangrove quantity should not be confused with quality. Lost old-growth mangrove forests, which harbor the most wildlife, are being replaced by less biodiverse and resilient new stands, he says. Contrary to the new studies, “the world’s mangroves are not bouncing back.”

A coral reef around the roots of mangrove trees in Raja Ampat, Indonesia. Wendy Mitchell / Mangrove Photography Awards 2026

Mangroves are unique trees, evolved with specialized roots that anchor in shallow, intertidal waters with slow currents, no frost, and plenty of sediment. Mangrove forests are critical biodiversity hotspots, supporting everything from barnacles to tigers, and are vital fish nurseries for the oceans. For coastal communities, they yield rich harvests of crabs and shellfish and form a protective barrier, absorbing winds and tidal surges during storms, and even moderating the energy of tsunamis. They also store large amounts of carbon — typically four times more than nearby tropical rainforests.

Zhang has recorded the biggest revivals in the river estuaries of northern Australia and river deltas in India. In each case, the new growth extends across more than 450 square miles. But the most surprising turnaround has been in Southeast Asian countries, which were once the scene of rapid mangrove destruction. Since 2010, they have accounted for more than 40 percent of global gains.

Myanmar is “still the most severely deforested country among major mangrove-holding nations,” says Zhang. But since 2010, its mangroves have grown in area by 10 percent. Indonesia tells a similar story. After major losses in past decades, due primarily to a boom in shrimp and fish aquaculture, mangroves have been stable since 2005, when the boom began to abate. The country remains home to around a quarter of the world’s mangroves.

“Some 65 percent of mangrove gains are in new places where mangroves have not grown before,” says an analyst.

So, what is going on? Why the dramatic upturn for a global ecosystem once considered all but doomed by human invasion and rising seas? The new remote-sensing analysis, despite its greater resolution, allows only tentative conclusions. “We don’t fully understand what is driving these gains,” says Bunting. His mapping cannot distinguish planted trees from natural recovery, for instance. But there is growing evidence that natural regeneration is powering the resurgence.

Sometimes, mangroves are recolonizing areas previously taken by humans but since abandoned. During the late 20th century, coastal communities across the tropics ripped out millions of acres of mangroves in East and Southeast Asia alone to make way for ponds where they raised fish and shrimp for lucrative international markets. But many of these ponds soon became unproductive through disease, pollution, or poor management, and were abandoned.

But such recolonization is only part of the story. “Some 65 percent of mangrove gains are in new places where mangroves have not grown before,” the State of the World’s Mangroves report finds. Sometimes climate change is helping extend the range of mangroves polewards. On the Mississippi Delta, they are overtaking salt marshes as warmer winters eliminate mangrove-killing frosts, restricting habitat for birds and foraging mammals that need open ground.

False-color satellite images show the growth of mangroves at the mouth of the Matamuhuri River in Bangladesh between 1990 and 2023. Source: Landsat imagery. Courtesy of Pete Bunting

The majority of the gains, however, “seem to occur in river mouths and deltas and are being driven by sediment coming off the land,” says Bunting. On reaching the ocean, the sediment settles, creating mudbanks that mangroves swiftly colonize. The unsettling paradox is that, in many cases, mangroves along coastlines are returning thanks to the destruction of their forest counterparts inland. The loss of trees and their roots destabilizes soils, causing erosion and the flow of sediment into rivers.

That is what has happened along the Yangon estuary in southern Myanmar. Part of the giant Irrawaddy Delta, the estuary stretches some 25 miles from the ocean to the country’s biggest city, Yangon. The estuary lost more than half its mangroves between 1988 and 2011 as rice farmers moved onto its shores and replaced mangroves with rice fields, erecting dikes to protect them from the salty water. But the mangroves have since made a dramatic comeback. By 2023, their coverage had increased almost tenfold to more than 13,000 acres, according to Phyu Phway Thant of the Myanmar Maritime University in Thanlyin, who has mapped the growth from satellite imagery.

The rice fields have not gone. Instead, almost all the growth was mangroves colonizing new mudbanks created from sediment dislodged by upstream sand mining and deforestation, which was driven by illegal logging and the expansion of agriculture along tributaries of the Yangon River.

Millions of dollars have been spent planting mangroves across the tropics, but “the majority of these projects have failed,” a report found.

This is not unusual. The growth of mudbanks in many estuaries has coincided with an increase in sediment brought down by rivers to coastal waters over the last 20 years, says the State of the World’s Mangroves report. Other examples include parts of the giant Amazon Delta in Brazil, the shores of peninsular Malaysia, and the North Island of New Zealand, which is at the southernmost limit of potential mangrove habitat.

“Rising sea levels should in theory restrict mangrove growth, as seas invade the intertidal areas where they grow,” says Lovelock, but at the mouths of many rivers, sediment deposition is creating land faster than the seas are engulfing it, creating new habitats that mangroves swiftly colonize. And once established, the dense networks of mangrove roots trap more sediment — enough, the State of the World’s Mangroves report concludes, to keep pace with current rising tides in many places.

Of course, this positive feedback loop can be confounded by upstream dams, which drastically reduce the amount of sediment being carried toward the ocean, stopping the growth of intertidal mud flats, and causing deltas to be drowned.

Shrimp farms in Prachuap Khiri Khan province in Thailand have displaced mangrove forests. Ingram Publishing

For this reason, there are serious concerns among ecologists about the fate of East Africa’s largest expanse of mangroves, on the delta of the River Rufiji in Tanzania. In recent years, new mangrove stands have grown on mudflats in the outer delta, says Bunting. But that growth could now abruptly halt. In August, the Tanzanian government completed the Julius Nyerere hydroelectric dam some 100 miles upstream. The environmental group WWF has estimated that the dam will trap most of the 16.6 million tons of sediment flowing down the river each year — initiating a cycle of delta retreat and mangrove loss.

The growth of new mangrove stands has been accompanied by a growing awareness among some governments and coastal communities of their value. This is especially true in Indonesia and other countries bordering the Indian Ocean that were hit by a tsunami in 2004 that killed more than 200,000 people. Villages that had kept their mangroves were much better protected than those that had converted them to fishponds.

A resulting fashion for planting new mangroves has had mixed results, however. Tens of millions of dollars have been spent on planting mangroves across the tropics in recent years, according to the NGO Wetlands International. But “the majority of these restoration projects have failed,” it said in a recent report. More than 80 percent of seedlings have died or been washed away by the tides.

The new mangrove stands colonizing the tropics may not be as resilient as their predecessors to climate change, an ecologist warns.

In response, some conservation groups have begun helping communities manage coastal landscapes to encourage natural regeneration. On the north shore of Java, villagers have erected some 10 miles of near-shore brushwood barriers to create calm water where seedlings cast off by mangroves have become established.

And in the West African state of Guinea-Bissau, Wetlands International is recruiting locals to encourage the natural return of mangroves to abandoned rice fields. “We open up dikes and clean the old natural canals” to allow water carrying mangrove seedlings from nearby stands to return, says Abdoulaye Ndiaye, who runs the program. Nature does the rest. More than 6,000 acres have been restored since 2015.

Meanwhile, the greener landscapes seen in satellite images do not necessarily indicate that biodiversity has recovered, says Uday Pimple of King Mongkut’s University of Technology in Bangkok, who has been doing extensive field research in the mangrove swamps of Thailand.

In Phang Nga province in western Thailand — an area where tin mining, charcoal burning, and shrimp farming previously decimated coastal mangroves — he found that 90 percent of mangrove recovery since the 1980s has been through the natural regeneration of a range of mangrove species, creating biodiverse forest. But restored mangrove forests in Trat province in eastern Thailand, which appear identical on satellite images, were largely planted with a single species of mangrove, resulting in much less biodiversity.

A man plants mangrove seedlings in Banda Aceh, Indonesia. Hand-planted mangroves rarely reach maturity. Chaideer Mahyuddin / AFP via Getty Images

Clearly, the prognosis for mangroves remains contested. Bunting says, “It is quite possible that the future trend will be similar to the last 15 years,” with gains continuing to exceed losses. And in a study of the likely fate of mangroves in a world 2 degrees Celsius warmer, Daniel Friess, a colleague of Zhang at Tulane University, found reasons to believe the trees could thrive. Because, at least in some places, they seem well able to keep pace with rising sea levels. Because increased rainfall will often increase soil erosion inland and sediment deposition along shorelines, giving mangroves even more room to expand. And because warmer temperatures should push mangroves further outside the tropics, replacing many more salt marshes in Australia and the southern U.S., for instance, for better or for worse.

But Duke argues that the new mangrove stands colonizing the tropics may not be as resilient as their predecessors to the more severe weather triggered by climate change. Or as useful in capturing and holding onto carbon. “They are immature stands, not fully developed in either biomass or biodiversity,” he says. That will leave them ever more vulnerable “as damaging [weather] events become more severe and more frequent.” Recent research appears to support his pessimistic presumption.

Field studies in China’s Hainan province found that mature mangrove forests recovered much more quickly from tropical cyclones, with their high winds, strong rainfall, and storm surges, compared with younger forests. The researchers stressed the importance of protecting old-growth mangroves rather than relying on new stands to replace them. Without such a strategy, humanity may yet face what Duke feared: “a world without mangroves.”

stories.title: The Pentagon’s Secret Budget
stories.summary: Trump’s proposed budget hides $1 trillion in military spending from the public by spreading it across disparate government agencies. The post The Pentagon’s Secret Budget appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Shutterstock

Originally published in TomDispatch .

News reports that next year’s U.S. military budget will top out at $1.5 trillion if President Donald Trump gets his way are misleading at best. The true total, if Trump’s proposal passes, could be at least $1 trillion higher.

Long before Trump took office, U.S. taxpayers have spent far more on the Pentagon — and its wars — than most know. For decades, Congress, the White House, and the Pentagon have hidden the military’s true cost through little-known bureaucratic practices and budgeting tricks. Journalists, academics, and think tank experts have, with rare exceptions, perpetuated the problem by repeating “official” numbers that don’t come close to telling the full story.

Data shows that the budget was already between $1.5 trillion and $1.8 trillion in the last full fiscal year, 2025, as detailed by a recent Project on Government Oversight, or POGO, report I co-authored. Trump’s requests would add another $781 billion, bringing the potential total to at least $2.581 trillion in 2027.

The troubling revelation that the government is misleading the public and effectively hiding hundreds of billions in military spending reflects the out-of-control nature of the Pentagon budget. It’s also the only sector of government spending that seems largely insulated from public scrutiny: Imagine the outrage if news broke that the government was hiding hundreds of billions in spending for public housing, Medicaid, or hunger prevention programs.

If Congress passes Trump’s full budget proposal, military spending will eat up around 75 percent of the discretionary budget Congress controls.

People have a right to know how much tax money goes to military spending. This is critical to debating the proper size of the military budget both on its own and compared to other spending priorities, particularly any program related to education or the social safety net. Understanding the military’s true cost means understanding where and how the government has been hiding the money.

Spending Hidden in Other Budgets

It’s difficult to untangle how much the country actually spends on the military in part because Congress pays for the armed forces and wars from many budgets rather than one. Beyond the agency controlling the military branches that Trump calls the “Department of War” (the official name is still the Department of Defense), hundreds of billions of dollars are effectively hidden in the budgets of at least 17 other government agencies and entities. In total, each of these additional sums are larger than what Congress appropriates for every non-military agency.

For years, TomDispatch and a small but mostly ignored group of budget experts have warned that tota l military spending is far higher than reported . Our new POGO report consolidates this prior work and five different methodologies for calculating the true military budget. The report shows a consensus that military spending was at least $1.5 trillion , with three of five methods reaching similar estimates of $1.7 trillion to $1.8 trillion.

The newest of the five methodologies provides the easiest way for anyone to see the hidden spending. The methodology uses data from a government website, USAspending.gov, the product of a 2006 law requiring the government “to give the American public access to information on how their tax dollars are being spent.” The site includes the closest thing to actual spending receipts, making it easier to identify military spending beyond the Department of War’s budget.

Let’s take a look at where the money’s hiding.

Hidden Nuclear Weapons Costs: $33.8 Billion

The most obvious place where Congress and the executive branch hide military spending is in the Department of Energy’s budget. That’s where taxpayers can find the bill for the U.S. nuclear weapons arsenal, which cost around $33.5 billion in 2025.

The Department of War controls and deploys these weapons, and their costs should properly be part of its budget, not rolled into the Department of Energy. While the Energy Department plays a role in overseeing the U.S. nuclear weapons stockpile, putting nuclear weapons spending in the DOE’s budget is like a city putting the costs of its police department’s bullets in its transportation department budget rather than in the police budget.

Another $300 million in nuclear weapons spending hides in the budgets of the Defense Nuclear Facilities Safety Board and the Army Corps of Engineers, bringing the total to nearly $34 billion.

Hidden Military Personnel (Veterans) Costs: $393.3 Billion

Taxpayers spend huge sums on the military in the Department of Veterans Affairs and related budgets. The existence of a separate veterans’ agency is a sleight of hand that leads the public to believe this is not military spending. It is. The only difference is the appropriation of money to still another agency.

To recruit and maintain armed forces, any government needs to pay its troops and offer sufficient long-term benefits (such as pensions, medical care in retirement, and survivor benefits) to encourage people to join and stay in a dangerous job that involves the risk of killing and being killed. These forms of long-term compensation are personnel costs, just as much as basic pay, and they should be counted as military spending. If a military fails to spend money to support vets, it’s unlikely to function for long. The Bureau of Pensions for veterans was originally part of the War Department (which was the name until 1947, long before Trump’s rebranding) and its budget until 1849 when Congress transferred the bureau to the Department of the Interior.

Funding for the Department of Veterans Affairs adds another $389.8 billion to the USAspending.gov methodology total. Almost $4 billion more in long-term spending on personnel hides in the budgets of the departments of Labor, Justice, and several others. All told, these sums reach a staggering $393.3 billion.

Coast Guard and Other “Homeland Security” Costs: $16.8 billion

Spending for an entire branch of the military, the Coast Guard, is concealed in the budget of the Department of Homeland Security rather than the Department of War. While DHS controls the Coast Guard during peacetime and the branch plays some non-military functions, the Coast Guard is one of the armed forces and is controlled by the Pentagon in wartime.

Excluding non-military activities (such as improving boat safety and cleaning up oil spills), Coast Guard spending adds nearly $14 billion to the total military budget. Additional DHS expenses for programs to counter weapons of mass destruction, radiological preparedness, cybersecurity, and other military spending add just under $3 billion, bringing this total to $16.8 billion.

The True Cost of the Department of War: $1.3 Trillion

The bulk of military expenditures still appear in the Department of War’s budget, which pays for the armed forces and the rest of the Pentagon’s sprawling bureaucracy, including all the weapons, salaries, some benefits, military construction, fuel, maintenance, operational expenses, and much more. USAspending.gov receipts show the Department of War alone spent $1.273 trillion in 2025. The Pentagon controlled another $480 million in spending that hid in the budgets of the State Department, the U.S. Agency for International Development , and the Department of Transportation.

Combined with the $444.8 billion tallied previously, total military spending hits $1.718 trillion. That’s more than double the military budget usually reported for 2025: the $850 billion Congress appropriated to the Department of War.

Total Military Spending by Agency (FY2025)

*No FY2025 spending. However, there was a $1 billion budget appropriation to the Executive Office of the President for “Submarine Security Activities, National Security Council.” The government also funded account line items in the Department of Agriculture budget to support the Air Force and Army.

Still Other Costs

The $1.7 trillion estimate for last year is conservative and still may be too low. While the War Department budget contains classified funding for the CIA, National Security Agency, and other intelligence agencies, the government may hide more intelligence spending elsewhere. NASA space research involves considerable military work, which could add another $10.5 billion, according to USAspending.gov data. Some would also count $1.9 billion in FBI salaries and expenses found in the Department of Justice budget.

Other experts consider much larger expenditures in the DHS budget to be military spending, given that department’s role in protecting the “ homeland ” and the increasingly militarized nature of Immigration and Customs Enforcement as well as Border Patrol . This would add at least $216.9 billion after excluding DHS’s Federal Emergency Management Agency spending. Alternate methodologies also include $211.9 billion in interest payments on the more than $40 trillion in national debt stemming from past military spending and wars.

You can add and subtract forms of spending that you think belong or don’t belong in the true total, thanks to the transparency of the POGO report’s methodologies. In total, these excluded sums could add another $441.2 billion to the USAspending.gov method’s prior total of $1.718 trillion for 2025.

Growing Opposition to Unchecked Pentagon Spending

POGO report’s conservative estimates of the FY2025 budget being $1.5 trillion to $1.8 trillion reveal that the true military budget for 2027 could hit $2.6 trillion if Congress gives Trump what he wants. This includes requested increases totaling $781 billion for just the Department of War ($500 billion), the Iran war ($70 billion), veterans ($144.9 billion), nuclear weapons ($53.9 billion), and the Coast Guard ($12.5 billion), let alone other smaller forms of hidden Pentagon spending.

When mind-numbing numbers like these reach the trillions, it can be tempting to think, What does it matter if it’s $1 trillion or $1.5 trillion or $2.6 trillion?

It helps me to remember that every single dollar spent on the Pentagon is a dollar not spent on our children, on healthcare, on affordable housing, on efforts to slow catastrophic climate change, and much more.

If Congress passes Trump’s full budget proposal, military spending will eat up around 75 percent of the discretionary budget Congress controls. Every dollar spent on the Pentagon is also a dollar more for Trump to continue waging his illegal, disastrous war on Iran and the funds to make good on his threats to attack Cuba and other countries.

Advocates for increased military spending will likely insist that more money is always needed, no matter today’s true total. That these Pentagon boosters have cited incorrect figures and helped mislead the public for decades raises serious questions about their credibility and the basis for their seemingly endless demands for more money.

Thankfully, there’s growing resistance to Trump’s proposals. Nearly 6 in 10 people nationwide believe even the official $1.5 trillion request is “too high,” according to a recent poll conducted by ReThink Media and the Costs of War Project at Brown University, a nonpartisan research group (where I’m a contributor). And Democrats appear to be listening : They’ve voted against Trump’s budget in unprecedented numbers as it winds through Congress. Some Republicans have also expressed concerns about supporting Trump’s proposal given fears about the rising national debt .

There are growin g calls to cut the Pentagon budget by hundreds of billions of dollars without touching salaries and benefits for troops and veterans. This would still leave the country with the world’s largest military budget by far and allow Congress to reallocate the savings to programs that improve the lives of everyday Americans.

The public needs a full, accurate accounting of the military. Congress could provide an annual True Total Military Budget that tallies all of the Pentagon’s spending in one place and stop hiding funding in other agencies’ budgets. Until this happens, journalists and analysts can help by explaining the full scale of spending and no longer repeating incomplete totals.

As Trump asks for the highest military budget in the history of the world and people continue to suffer the effects of his war with Iran — which has killed and injured thousands, increased the price of gas and groceries , and risks even greater catastrophic harm globally — it’s time to have an informed debate about how much the country really needs to spend on its military.

stories.body:
What comes after the dissolution of the liberal world order.

Alden Young is an associate professor of history and global affairs at Yale University. He was a 2021-22 Berggruen Institute Fellow.

Muez Ali is an adjunct professor at Georgetown University in Qatar and honorary research fellow at University College London.

This work is supported by the Cross-Border Conflict Evidence, Policy and Trends (XCEPT) research program, funded by UK International Development. The views and opinions expressed are those of the authors and do not necessarily represent those of the UK government.

Sudan has often served as a mirror for judging the health of the liberal world order because it has repeatedly been a laboratory for multilateral interventions to prevent atrocities and stabilize the humanitarian situation.

During the second Sudanese civil war, which stretched from 1983 to 2005, an estimated more than two million people died. In Darfur during the first decade of the 2000s, international observers estimated that 300,000 people died and another 2-3 million people were displaced.

At the time, finding a solution to Sudan’s conflicts was a priority for the United States and the coalitions it galvanized. For instance, Sudan’s second civil war came to an end only after intense mediation by the troika of the United States, the United Kingdom and Norway, as well as Sudan’s African neighbors, in 2005. The level of Western concern and diplomatic resources mobilized to intervene in Sudan’s conflicts in the early 2000s feels almost unimaginable today.

In the 2000s, Sudan hosted two massive UN peacekeeping missions : the more than 13-year-long African Union-United Nations Hybrid Operation in Darfur, which ended in 2020 and the more than six-year-long United Nations Mission in the Sudan, which ended in 2011. The goals of these missions were to prevent genocide in Darfur and to guarantee the implementation of the peace agreement ending the civil war between the Sudanese People’s Liberation Movement/Army and the government in Khartoum. This mission, which included approximately 10,000 soldiers and numerous civilian authorities, ended with a referendum on the independence of South Sudan in 2011. A few months later South Sudan was welcomed by the international community as the newest country in the world.

It was in this context — of the international efforts to end Sudan’s civil wars and the resulting mass displacements — that South Sudanese diplomat Francis Mading Deng developed the idea of “ sovereignty as responsibility .” Deng served as the Special Representative of the United Nations Secretary-General on internally displaced persons from 1992 to 2004, and many experts credit Deng’s idea of sovereignty as responsibility as the intellectual genesis of the international principle of the Responsibility to Protect . The UN General Assembly’s adoption of the Responsibility to Protect (R2P) principles in 2005 marked a high-water point for the legitimacy of the liberal world order. R2P, as formulated by Deng and others, tried to balance sovereignty as a state’s right to non-interference with the international community’s duty to ensure that a state protects the welfare of its own citizens.

Today, the conflict in Sudan can be described as a world war in microcosm. The numbers are massive and stark, making it hard to comprehend the magnitude of the tragedy unfolding there. At least 14 million people have been internally displaced since the latest round of fighting in April 2023, according to the United Nations Refugee Agency. Meanwhile, there are at least 4.4 million Sudanese refugees who have fled the country, many to neighboring countries like Chad, Egypt and South Sudan, which can ill-afford to support this influx. Three years on, intense fighting persists in Sudan’s central region of Kordofan, in Darfur and in its southeastern Blue Nile state.

In one of the most widely discussed recent commentaries on the crisis in Sudan — a conflict often overshadowed despite its horrific violence by other wars — the American journalist and historian Anne Applebaum wrote that “no statistics can express the sense of pointlessness, of meaninglessness, that the war has left behind” after she reported from behind the lines of both the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and their opponents, the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). In the face of the physical destruction of cities like Khartoum, Applebaum declared the conflict the most nihilistic on Earth, writing with a tinge of hopelessness that “the liberal world order has already ended in Sudan, and there isn’t anything to replace it.”

In many ways, what is happening in Sudan represents the international community’s abandonment of the longstanding principles of the liberal world order, particularly by the West. Instead, Sudan has become the plaything for a wide array of actors stretching across the Middle East and Africa, to Russia and Ukraine, and as far afield as Colombia. After the Trump administration’s cuts to organizations like the U.S. Agency for International Development, even the commitment to prevent the spread of famine has declined. Applebaum ended her piece by lamenting that Sudan is now a victim of an anarchic, post-American world. A world that has yet to fully take shape in which “colonialism is long past, the Cold War has ended,” and the international order has irreparably broken down.

“Today, the conflict in Sudan can be described as a world war in microcosm.”

But what is taking place in Sudan and elsewhere is not the emergence of anarchy; it is a return to precolonial patterns. Many observers have mistakenly assumed the former because of what the historian Richard Reid calls the “ foreshortening of African history ,” by which he means “the detachment of Africa’s turbulent present — and its recent past — from deeper patterns of both change and continuity.” Perhaps no country has suffered more from the reification of the colonial past by social scientists and modernizing elites alike than the Congo, once known as Zaire.

At the end of the 19th century, Henry Morten Stanley earned the name Bula Matari or the breaker of rocks, for “his feat of driving a caravan of porters bearing dismantled steamers over the torturous terrain between the Zaire River estuary and the vast navigable watercourses extending inward from Kinshasa.” As Zala Lusibu N’Kanza, the first woman to hold the position of minister in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, notes, “for all Bakongo the name of Bula Matari signified terror.” The precolonial was smashed in the wake of an ascendant and modernizing colonial and post-colonial state. For the founding generation of American political scientists like the late Crawford Young, the political, economic and social institutions of the precolonial period were left in ruins because they lacked the resilience to create an alternative to the modernizing state.

A Return To The Pre-Colonial Era

Despite the depths of the human tragedy playing out across northeast Africa — engulfing not only Sudan but South Sudan, Ethiopia, Eritrea, Somalia and Somaliland — Applebaum’s post-American world is not just chaos. Clear patterns are emerging even amid the violence of state fracture. One of the clearest is the development of political and trade patterns resembling those of the pre-colonial era. The long dominance of the colonial state was not the result of smashing African societies, as American political scientists long suspected. Just as the chaos marring the post-colonial period is not a result of ethnic rivalries. Rather, the endurance of colonialism in countries like Sudan is a product of the legacies of its infrastructure.

The peculiar durability of the infrastructure built during European control of the Nile basin resulted from a set of historical conjunctures. In his new book, “The Alibi of Capital: How We Broke the Earth to Steal the Future on the Promise of a Better Tomorrow,” the political theorist Timothy Mitchell argues that around the turn of the 20th century a new ability to discount the future was invented. Mitchell considers this ability a political technology “derived from the fact that time can be controlled — by the construction of a political apparatus that will reliably capture and colonize the future.” While this sounds incredibly abstract, Mitchell goes on to explain that:

“That the scale and extension of transportation lines and energy networks, along with urban development, irrigation projects, and other immense schemes, depended not just on material durability but upon the durable arrangements of law, authority, compulsion, and justification.”

Sudan, though often imagined as a colonial backwater, was the site of one of the British Empire’s largest investments in industrial agriculture ever. The giant Gezira irrigated agricultural scheme, one of the only monuments to colonialism visible from outer space, was originally planned in the 1920s to irrigate more than a million acres. British officials spoke openly of the Gezira Scheme’s potential to be a second man-made Nile Delta, a giant cotton farm for the Empire. From the 1920s until the scheme ran into financial problems in the 1970s, the railways, dams, ports and even Sudan’s labor force were geared to serve this project, not to mention the country’s financial and economic infrastructure.

This changed in the 1990s as the oil sector rose to prominence, but even then, pipelines and refineries tended to be located according to patterns established during the colonial era. These patterns endured in part because irrigation canals and railways cut into the earth and were reinforced with steel, and because Sudan integrated into global financial markets through loans for investments backed by access to export markets. Originally, it was cotton, later crude oil and now gold.

The Fragile Liberal International Order

When the Princeton political scientist G. John Ikenberry wrote about the liberal international order, he remarked that, “there is an optimist assumption lurking in liberal internationalism that states can overcome constraints and cooperate to solve security dilemmas, pursue collective action, and create an open, stable system.” Yet Ikenberry also admits that the system’s collective nature was always more aspirational than practical. Ikenberry admits that since 1945 the United States has served as the owner and operator of this system and has been afforded special privileges and responsibilities. Applebaum describes the chaos that unfolds in Sudan once the United States is no longer willing to bear its historic burden. Read Noema in print.

“Clear patterns are emerging even amid the violence of state fracture. One of the clearest is the development of political and trade patterns resembling those of the pre-colonial era.”

But what if what looks like chaos is simply the dissolution of the political orders that made colonial and postcolonial state investments durable? While cotton and crude petroleum are different commodities, the central state could largely control their export, either by managing production directly or by issuing licenses for production and sale to favored clients. The boom in gold exports from Sudan since 2013 is remarkable because of the state’s utter inability to control the trade. For Sudan, the tragedy is magnified by the almost 200% rise in gold prices during that period, meaning the Sudanese state lost out on this windfall due to incapacity and now war. Part of the challenge for Sudanese authorities is that artisanal gold production , unlike control of oilfields and pipelines or cotton irrigation, lacks the central infrastructural chokepoints the colonial and postcolonial state had become so adept at taxing.

The other dilemma for the Sudanese state is the regional collapse of the taboo against dealing with subnational actors. As a result, gold from the mines of Darfur often ends up in the souks of Dubai without ever passing through the central government. Similarly, Sudanese soldiers guarding the Saudi-Yemeni border can be hired and deployed without ever contracting with the SAF. The RSF, a paramilitary-slash-merchant company, carries out many of these transactions, managing large portions of Sudan on behalf of its investors.

Precolonial Patterns Return In Contemporary Guises

What looks like chaos reveals patterns. In the 3 ½ years since fighting broke out between the SAF and the RSF, new trade and military supply routes have become increasingly visible. During the first few decades following Sudan’s independence in 1956, most economic activity flowed from the provinces to Khartoum, then along the railroad lines to Port Sudan on the Red Sea. The government earned most of its revenue by taxing the imports and exports that followed this well-trodden route. During the first two years of fighting, the Rapid Support Forces controlled Khartoum and did everything in their power to break the old colonial trade route. During this time, Sudan’s government retreated to Port Sudan, and the RSF set up a rival capital in Nyala in southern Darfur.

Inadvertently, the war revealed older patterns of state formation from the 19th century. Sudan’s city of Suakin and its other Red Sea ports claimed allegiance to a distant Ottoman government and resisted incorporation into the Kingdom of Sennar, to say nothing of Darfur. Elites in Suakin often sought incorporation into the Ottoman province of the Hijaz or Aden on the Arabian Peninsula. This pattern threatened to repeat itself when Sudan’s government was again temporarily forced to relocate to Port Sudan after Khartoum fell in 2023.

But perhaps more dramatically, the war saw the re-emergence of old trade routes to the north, west and south of Darfur. With the SAF in control of Port Sudan, the RSF began to turn to the old trade routes across the desert, the most famous of which was the Darb El Arba’īn, or “40 Day Road,” leading from northern Darfur to Asyut in southern Egypt. Other trade routes led north into Libya, where the RSF is suspected to have established bases under the protection of the Libyan militia leader who rules the eastern part of the country, Khalifa Haftar. Similarly, the trading routes from southern Darfur into South Sudan have been reactivated to resupply the RSF. These routes often end in Uganda, Kenya and the Central African Republic. All outside the control of the center.

The new prominence of the old trade routes was capped by the declaration of TASIS , or the Sudan Founding Alliance, of a new government in April 2025, exactly two years after the outbreak of the war. Speaking from Nairobi, Kenya’s capital, TASIS leaders tried to solidify an alliance between the RSF, parts of the Sudanese People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N), a militant group and political party, and the leadership of the Baggara confederation. The Baggara includes more than six million Arab and African people stretching from southern Kordofan to Lake Chad.

The RSF’s organization, founded in 2013 — with the Darfurian Arab family of its leader Muhammad Hamdan Daglo Musa at its center — itself echoes an episode from the late 19th century. The first is the creation of a private-merchant empire by al-Zubayr Rahma al-Mansur, usually known as Zubayr Pasha . Originally a lackluster merchant assistant for an Egyptian trader, by the 1860s Zubayr had established one of the largest merchant companies operating in what we today refer to as South Sudan.

His operations were described in a remembrance in the “Middle East Monitor” as such: “[He sent] men ‘through the lands of the Dinka, Jur and Bongo, the company reached the Golo, then living between the Kuru and Kpongo rivers.’ They purchased ostrich feathers and ivory for trade in Khartoum, Cairo and beyond.” By the 1870s, he had grown from a successful trader into the ruler of a territory often called Deim Zubayr, controlling a large area of present-day South Sudan’s Bahr al-Ghazal and Darfur with an army of some 12,000 soldiers, many of whom were enslaved. According to the historian Tsega Etefa , writing in the Journal of Oromo Studies:

“What if what looks like chaos is simply the dissolution of the political orders that made colonial and postcolonial state investments durable?”

“By the late 1860s, al Zubayr was ‘the most prominent and successful of the merchant princes operating in the Bahr al-Ghazal.’ He traded in slaves and ivory; however, antislavery movements by Egyptian and European explorers in the Nile Valley began to put pressure on him. Therefore, ‘he arranged with the Baqqara tribes of southern Darfur for his slave caravans to pass through their territory northward, bypassing the Nile.’ Toward the end of the 1860s, ‘he attained the position of practically an independent ruler.’ The Egyptian government’s expeditionary force ‘was completely defeated by him, and the Egyptian authorities, realizing with what a commanding character they were confronted, made him Governor of the district.’”

Initially, Zubayr’s base was in the southern borderlands between Darfur and Bahr al-Ghazal. Darfur, as an independent political entity, was not conquered until 1874, when Zubayr’s forces achieved what the Ottoman-Egyptian armies of Muhammad Ali had been unable to do in 1821: conquering the Fur Sultanate at its capital of El Fasher. The parallels with the RSF appear to write themselves. These became particularly notable when the RSF took El Fasher after months of siege at the end of October 2025. In the process, the RSF captured the last major stronghold in Darfur and solidified their ability to resupply to the north through Libya and to the south across the expanse of South Sudan into East Africa.

Yet another echo of the 19th century was the emergence of Kordofan as a contested region. The armies of Muhammad Ali, de facto ruler of Egypt from 1805 to 1848, partially pacified the region in the decades after the 1821 invasion from Egypt, but could not maintain stable control. In many ways, this resembles the situation in Kordofan today, where cities like El-Obeid , with a population over 600,000, remain under frequent attack as rival forces contend to dominate the region. Still, the 19th-century echoes perhaps become clearest in the relative autonomy of the SPLM-N, a political party and militant group with its strongholds based in southern Kordofan.

The SPLM-N has been both a broker and spoiler for South Sudan since its secession in 2011. The flat plains were easily conquered, but the Nuba Mountains were very difficult to ultimately control. One faction, SPLM-N Al-Hilu, which mostly controls the areas around the Nuba Mountains in South Kordofan, sided with the RSF, while another faction, SPLM-N Agar, which controls parts of the Blue Nile state, has sided with the SAF.

In the process, the two groups have maintained the autonomy of the border regions between the RSF, SAF and South Sudan. A borderland organization more interested in preserving its own autonomy than in the outcome of the war has found itself operating on both sides of the conflict. In this way, they are implementing strategies with other surprising parallels in the past, such as the Kingdom of Taqali , a kingdom in the northeastern Nuba Mountains of Sudan that flourished between about 1780 and 1884, with relative autonomy that extended well into Sudan’s post-independence period until 1969.

Our research in the Sudan Collection at the University of Bergen in Norway shows that during the 19th century, Taqali leaders used a similar strategy of seeking protection and recognition from both the waning states of Darfur and Sennar — pledging vassalage to both simultaneously as they worked to maintain autonomy.

The breakdown of the Sudanese state we are witnessing today is also not random. Rather, along with the retreat of the liberal world order, we are witnessing the reappearance of political orders that last manifested themselves with such clarity in the 19th century. These patterns repeat because they are based on trade and political and economic linkages that do not rely on the infrastructure built during the colonial period. The durability of this infrastructure has decayed as the institutions of the liberal world order that maintained it have crumbled. In the place of the patterns of trade, infrastructure and political order that once felt like inevitable parts of the postcolonial world, we are witnessing the reappearance of the older routes of exchange.

For instance, we see the re-emergence of the Trans-Saharan routes, the trading routes into East and Central Africa and East-West connections across the Sahel and the Red Sea. In South Africa, there are calls to dissolve the Union of South Africa, which in 1910 joined the British Cape Colony with the independent Boer republics of the Transvaal and Free State as well as Natal. Yemen has been redividing for over a decade now in ways that are reminiscent of the 19th century, and of course Russian aggression has called into question the stability of eastern Europe’s borders.

These are just a few examples of how the stability that defined the second half of the 20th century cannot be taken for granted. As we think of what models might best explain statecraft after the liberal order, it increasingly makes sense to look at the 19th-century map as an example of political competition and shifting boundaries.
