stories.title: Angry scenes and protests at Senedd as Reform call for ban on Muslim face coverings
stories.summary: Members of Reform called for Muslim religious face coverings, such as the burka, to be banned.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
After the debate a number of Plaid Cymru and Labour politicians took part in a protest on the Senedd steps - with Safa Elhassan addressing those gathered

Published 21 October 2026

There were bad-tempered and dramatic exchanges in the Senedd on Wednesday night as members of Reform called for Muslim religious face coverings, such as the burka, to be banned.

Politicians from the party said they were "anti-British", allowed Muslim women to hide their identities and suggested they represented an "alien culture".

Plaid Cymru and Labour politicians responded with disdain - Deputy First Minister Sioned Williams raised the Nuremberg Laws of 1930s Germany and how they led to the extermination of Jews.

The Muslim Council of Wales described "disturbingly authoritarian attitudes" - Reform's Jason O'Connell accused the group of trying to "silence" the debate.

There was no vote on the topic. The Senedd would have no power to ban face coverings.

A protest, including some Members of the Senedd (MSs), took place on the Senedd steps.

It is the latest heated debate in the Senedd on a Wednesday prompted by Reform MSs - previous include a discussion about the Nation of Sanctuary and calls for foreign nationals to be banned from house shares .

A niqab is a form of a veil used by Muslim women

Reform UK has previously said it would ban face coverings in public places , including burkas and balaclavas, if it won power at the next Westminster election.

Opening the debate to a nearly full chamber, Reform UK MS for Pontypridd Cynon Merthyr, Jason O'Connell, began by speaking about young men wearing balaclavas.

"From Newport to Rhyl, balaclava-clad young men, often dangerously riding illegal e-bikes, have been fuelling anti-social behaviour and making our streets feel unsafe," he said.

"For these individuals, face coverings are a way to conceal their identity, to make it harder for authorities to hold them accountable.

"And while governments across the UK turn a blind eye to this, Reform says enough is enough now, face coverings have no place in British and Welsh society."

Turning to the burka, O'Connell, who called Wednesday's debate, said: "We have no issue or problem with Islam or Muslims."

With opposing members heckling as he spoke, he added: "We do have an issue with people living amongst our communities hiding their identities.

"We say the same thing to protesters that cover their face, whatever their political persuasion."

Jason O'Connell called the short debate on face coverings late on Wednesday night

Amid frequent interruptions, fellow Reform MS Francesca O'Brien told the Senedd that face coverings, including the burka, were "anti-British".

"Not all cultures are equal," she said. "We cannot continue to import alien cultures into this country and expect integration.

"Oppressive beliefs are totally at odds with our history and culture.

"Banning these coverings is simple, common sense."

Reform MS Joe Martin said the burka and niqab were "two of the many ways in which fundamentalist Islam is uniquely incompatible with Western civilization".

"We can't even see the faces of thousands of people who've moved here. If two Muslim women live in the same street and they both wear burkas, how are we meant to tell them apart?

"Assimilation means losing religious face coverings and to encourage that they should be banned."

The burka is a veil worn by some Muslim women that covers the face and body, often leaving a mesh screen to see through.

It covers more of the face than a niqab, a veil that leaves the area around the eyes clear.

In comparison, a hijab is a headscarf that in the West most commonly covers the head and neck but leaves the face clear.

A protest took place on the steps of the Senedd before the debate on Wednesday

Williams said the debate was a "shameful" end to a "sad day" that began with the commemoration of the Aberfan disaster .

Looking at the Reform members, she accused them of "conflating the intimidating behaviour of thugs and those whose protest can descend into disorder and violence, often in demonstrations directed against migrants or Muslims, with the very people who are targeted by that intimidating behaviour".

"I do not accept that a face covering worn by an individual for religious reasons means they don't share British or Welsh values," she said.

"Nor should we suggest that someone belongs any less, because their religious practice differs from that of others."

Williams added: "The Jewish people of 1930s Germany were subject to the Nuremberg Laws, which stated they were no longer German, laws which led to their persecution and extermination by the state that stripped them of the Germaness.

"Who decides that a woman who [has] a face covering is less British or less Welsh?"

The comments led to angry protests and finger pointing from the Reform benches.

A point of order was raised by a member of the party asking the presiding officer if the comments were appropriate.

The presiding officer Huw Irranca-Davies said he was "always happy" to review the record of proceedings, but did not make a ruling.

Williams said she was making a "statement of fact".

Carrie Harper, Plaid MS for Fflint Wrecsam, told Reform UK: "How on earth can you claim to stand up for women when you are trying to dictate what Muslim women can and cannot wear?"

Plaid MS Kiera Marshall, for Caerdydd Penarth, said a Muslim woman in her constituency was subject to a "physical, violent attack in broad daylight".

"The attacker shouted at her about removing her headscarf and continued to do exactly this while physically assaulting her," she said.

"This is just one example of an increasingly common occurrence when Muslim women are being targeted.

"This is exactly what the rhetoric that Reform is peddling is doing."

Labour's Huw Thomas said he had not heard Reform condemn "the masked mobs who stormed RNLI stations across of South Coast, last month".

A lifeboat station in Portsmouth went out of service in September, following anti-migrant protests.

Following the debate, Dr Abdul Azim Ahmed of the Muslim Council of Wales said: "This debate demonstrated the disturbingly authoritarian attitudes members of Reform UK hold, coupled with dangerously ultra nationalist attitudes about culture and belonging."

Suwayba Hussein accused Reform of using the debate "to push Islamophobia"

Ahead of the debate, a protest took place on the Senedd steps, with Plaid Cymru and Labour MSs later joining them.

One of those taking part, Suwayba Hussein from Cardiff, accused Reform of using the debate "to push Islamophobia".

"We're trying to just live our lives, we integrate really well, and this is just going to increase the Islamophobia that we see in modern-day society," she said.

"The Reform party are a racist party, and this is another way of them pushing their racism into mainstream debate."

During the debate, O'Connell said that accusations of racism and Islamophobia against Reform were "tired, ineffective, and clearly wildly inaccurate".

Opposition politicians and parties are able to use the Senedd on a Wednesday to raise issues that they want discussed, and individual members can trigger so-called "short debates".

Since the election, Reform - which is the second largest group in the Welsh Parliament - has used Wednesdays to raise topics that have resulted in angry debates.

The topic of short debates must not contain language considered by the presiding officer to be disorderly, discriminatory or offensive.

BBC Wales was told before the debate proceeded that the Senedd's presiding officer, Irranca-Davies, did not consider the title - "full-face coverings are against British values" - to be against the guidance.

stories.title: Interoperability vs. Security: Why not both?
stories.summary: An open internet where people can freely build, share, and remix each other's work is a powerful engine of grassroots innovation we’ve all benefited from. In recent decades, however, corporations have taken control of an increasing share of this work, giving them a greater ability to stifle challengers and limit our choices. When regulators address this by mandating that tech giants play fair by requiring interoperability, the gatekeepers respond with a tired refrain: Playing fair puts users’ security at risk. Unfortunately for these trillion-dollar companies, this gotcha isn’t the end of the conversation. Regulators can ensure that meaningful choice and security thrive. Lawmakers have been catching up, recognizing that the best way to rein in big tech is to require these oligopolies to open up their platforms to independent developers. As we explained six years ago , mandating interoperability helps prevent the misuse of people’s data and enables more privacy-respecting alternatives. Tech giants, in contrast, have been arguing that our data is safer when they have exclusive control. Tech Giants Claim Interoperability Means Insecurity The European Union’s Digital Markets Act (DMA) put interoperability into law under Article 6(7): “gatekeeper shall allow providers of services and providers of hardware, free of charge, effective interoperability with” a designated Core Platform Service they operate. The language describes an unambiguous requirement to remediate vendor lockouts and anti-competitive behavior of the major service operators—it is not optional. Apple claimed that enforcing this obligation in mobile app stores would put their customers at risk and do irreparable harm to trust in their brand. It’s an argument reminiscent of Apple’s fight against the right to repair , and in both instances the company is fighting to maintain its restrictive ecosystem to stop people from finding better deals elsewhere. Apple has long cultivated a more corporate-controlled experience with the iPhone, but this argument is now also being used for the relatively-more-open Android devices from Google. stories.title: EFF’s State Legislative Agenda to End ALPR Mass Surveillance
stories.summary: Police agencies across the U.S. have deployed Automated License Plate Readers (ALPRs) to capture images of passing vehicles along with time, date, and GPS coordinates. While the technology itself isn’t new (ALPRs have existed in various forms for more than 50 years , and in the U.S. since 1998 ), the surveillance landscape has shifted dramatically. Rapid advances in artificial intelligence and national data sharing have transformed police ALPRs into an interconnected, nationwide tracking network. It is pitched to city councils by law enforcement and private vendors like Flock Safety, Motorola Solutions (Vigilant), and Axon as an essential tool for solving violent crime. In reality, it is an inherently dangerous infrastructure of mass surveillance. Since 2012 , EFF has worked with others to expose the severe digital rights harms of ALPR systems. For example, we’ve recently documented how these camera networks allow law enforcement to search for immigrants , track peaceful protesters , target Romani communities , and track women seeking reproductive healthcare . Police also routinely use ALPRs for low-level matters like enforcing school residency requirements or investigating noise complaints . Many officers also use ALPR databases to stalk past romantic partners . Recent EFF analysis revealed officers using the system without legitimate justification—logging search reasons like "LOL" and "LMAO." Understandably, the public backlash to police ALPR technology is accelerating, and state lawmakers across the country are taking action. New Hampshire enacted the nation’s first state law on ALPR use in 2007, but technological advances and misconduct have driven even more recent legislative action. stories.title: EFF Launches Guide to Help Parents and Youth Protect Privacy Online
stories.summary: Guide Includes Easy, Quick Ways To Identify and Protect Against Online Threats SAN FRANCISCO – The Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) has published “ Online Privacy for Parents and Youth ,” a new guide to help families protect themselves online. "Parents don’t need to be technology experts to help their children navigate the digital world safely” said EFF Public Interest Technology Director Babette Ngene. “At EFF, we believe in empowering families with the knowledge and confidence to make informed decisions about their digital lives. It’s about meeting families where they are and giving parents the guidance they need to have meaningful conversations with their children about digital safety, based on what works best for their families.” EFF launches this crucial resource as state and local governments consider enacting well-meaning but ill-advised laws that cut young people off from essential information and experiences, particularly harming vulnerable youth and marginalized groups who often find safety in supportive online communities they can't access offline. Such laws also entail age gating, which compromises the privacy of all internet users and stifles young users’ ability to learn, grow, and express themselves. “Deciding how to help your young people use the internet—including engaging with video games, social media, web search, and everything else—is a complicated topic that touches on many different skillsets and ideas,” said EFF Senior Security and Privacy Activist Thorin Klosowski. “But ultimately it's up to families – not governments – to decide when and how to engage with these sorts of questions.” Each young person has unique needs, and, just like their wardrobe, that changes as they age. Parents can engage in thoughtful planning to find the best, most efficient solutions that evolve along with their children. EFF’s guide is about helping parents explore their concerns and identify the threats their children face – like trusting AI chatbots or sharing personal information with strangers – and then determine steps they and their children can take to mitigate those risks while still using the games, educational materials, and communication platforms that help them grow.
